MORE DEVILTRY.
An Attempt at Robbery and Assassination at Chillicothe.
Chillicothe, Mo., June 11, 2 p.m. —
This morning at 4 o'clock, a supposed attempt was made to rob the ticket office of the Hannibal and St. Joseph railroad at this place, by a party of negroes, whose depredations upon public and private property are becoming to frequent to be much longer endured by a civilized community. At the hour named a number of these characters had congregated at the stock pen, nearly opposite from the depot, while two of their number were appointed to begin their devilish work Henry Smith, night operator, had just opened the ticket office, which is located about twenty feet from the telegraph office and north of the passenger waiting room, while Fred Tucker, the night assistant, was left in charge of the instruments. Approaching the door one of them urged the other, in loud words, to "go in and send the dispatch." Entering, he asked one or two common place questions and then, with an oath, drew a revolver and fired, the ball entering the right cheek near the corner of the mouth and coming out back of the ear. Tucker was seated in a chair at the time this shot was fired and jumped to catch the assassin, who ran out on the platform. Closing the door, Tucker wheeled around to get his revolver, and in doing so, was in the act of raising his right hand to the wound when the accomplice fired at him through the window, the shot taking effect at the second joint of the thumb, the ball lodging near the wrist joint and disabling him from using a revolver. Parties near the depot, hearing the firing, hurried to the scene of conflict, which frightened the gang away and probably prevented any further attempt at life or property. Mr. Tucker is one of the finest young men in the city, and his friends, to the number of 100 or more, including city and county officials, are in close pursuit of these thieves and assassins. Tucker's wounds are not dangerous.

CRIME RAMPANT. TWO NEGROES, WITH MURDER AND ROBBERY IN THEIR HEARTS, SHOOT A TELEGRAPH OPERATOR AT A CHILLICOTHE RAILROAD DEPOT. AND ARE CAUGHT AFTER AN EXCITING CHASE AND LODGED IN JAIL, JUST IN TIME TO SAVE THEIR NECKS. A MOB OF 100 MEN CALL FOR THEM AT THE DEAD HOUR OF MIDNIGHT. BUT OUR BRAVE SHERIFF MANTAINS THE SUPREMACY OF THE LAW.
Sunday morning about 3:45 o'clock, two young negro men, Alex Murray and Charles Shelby, entered the H. & St. Joe telegraph office in this city and told Fred Tucker, who was there learning telegraphy, that they wanted to send a dispatch. Tucker who was in a recining position on the table and was in a doze, answered, "all right, write it out," and thinking they were joking, did not get up. The negroes went out but Murray come back in a few minutes and saying "get up you —," pulled a revolver and shot Tucker in the face the ball entering near the mouth and coming out just below the ear on the same side. Tucker jumped up and called for Henry Smith who was in the ticket office, when Shelby fired through

from the second shot, and was received when he put his hand on his wounded cheek, but from an examination of the telegraph office and the course of the two shots, it is thought that the first shot must have inflicted both wounds, which could easily have been done if he was resting on his elbow. The alarm was given and Fred was accompanied to his hotel, the Marcum House. By ten o'clock dozens of men were scouring the country south and east of town. George Graham and Policeman Tom Anderson got on the track of Shelby and in the afternoon overhauled him in Linn county, about two and a half miles north of Meadville and 12 or 13 miles east of here. They brought him back, took him to the Marcum House where he was clearly identified by Tucker, and then hastened with him to the jail, arriving there less than a minute ahead of a large and excited crowd.

The search for Murray was continued and about supper time he was found in an empty house in north-west part of town just across the street from his mother's residence. W. T. Folwell, Wallace Brown and L. S. Bearce entered the house through a window and discovered Murray asleep on the floor. Folwell grabbed his hands, Wallace Brown seized his feet and Bearce grabbed him by the arms. His pistol was taken from him and he was hurried to the jail as it was known two ropes were taken out there by some of the searchers.

THE SHERIFF'S NIGHT CALLERS.

About 1 o'clock, Sunday night, about 100 men called at the jail and demanded Murray and Shelby. In the jail were Sherin Leeper, his wife and his sons, Dr. Carl Leeper, of Catawba, and Willie Leeper. They were all upstairs, but the sheriff, who was down stairs in the south east room. He raised the window, threw open the shutters and calmly reasoned with his callers and at the same time informed them that he would kill the first man who attempted to enter the door. About this time the street lamp was shot out and one near the sheriff fired his pistol in the air. Most of the crowd thinking Leeper fired the shot, fled precipitately. The others soon dispersed and everything was quiet the remainder of the night.

THEY STOLE FOUR HORSES or at least that is the supposition. On Saturday night two horses were stolen at Utica from F. Bonderer and two from Green Cooper at the Water Tank between here and Utica. Sunday morning, Geo. Hoskins residing this side of the river and near the Spring Hill road, started to his barn to feed his horses when two negroes came out and shot at him and decamped after Hoskins had snapped a shot gun at them.

Park Giltner Sunday morning about 7:30 while on his way to a pasture just north of town, saw Alex Murray coming in from the country, but not knowing he was wanted paid no attention to him.

The horses were all recovered Sunday. Two in the bottom west of town and the other two on the Spring Hill road in the vicinity of J. H. Abshire's. So it is pretty certain that Murray and Snelby with perhaps some accomplices stole the horses. A colored man by the name of Hampton Arnold has been arrested on suspicion of being one of the thieves and is now in jail. The revolver found on Murray when arrested is one which was stolen from Henry Leeper's hardware store a few nights ago.

Murray and Shelby are not strangers in our jail. Murray has been in the penitentiary; was tried in January for burglarizing Fowler's saloon and was acquitted, the evidence being slight, but subsequent events proved him guilty. He is the son of Sarah Bryan who was a slave of the late Thomas Bryan. His brother George was hung in the southern suburbs of th is city about 9 years ago by a vigilance committee from south of the river for outraging a little girl.

Shelby was tried at the recent session of Circuit Court for stealing a pocket book and money from Gus. Henry's house one night last summer, but was discharged, there being no evidence of his guilt, though he was undoubtedly guilty.

ELDER J. F. JORDAN, of Daviess county, who was the Greenback nominee for the legislature in 1880, in conversation with us recently, said they expected to run Burrows for Congress in the third district if he would make the race.

The Inference Between Low Wages and Low Cost of Living and High Wages and High Cost of Living.

L. H. Weller, chairman of Greenback State Committee of Iowa, in Des Moines Tribune.

We see that volume of money, in circulation, determines the commercial value, (or purchasing power) of each "unit" or dollar. This being true, let us inquire what benefit increased volume of money would be to the producers of wealth—(for labor produces all wealth, except that which "The First Great Cause"—God—grants)—the farmer, mechanic, artisan, wage-worker—to those who have "nothing to sell" (?)—except labor.

Grant me Beecher Bread and no butter price—one dollar per day; seventy five cents of this to provide a home, and feed, clothe and educate the children, and help christianize society by building school houses pay taxes, recreation, contribute to charities and pay the minister, etc. I have left, as a mathematical proposition, just twenty-five cents with which to buy my home, pay interest on my indebtedness, cancel mortgages and notes, and my annual share of the state and national bonds and interest thereon.

Now, if by reducing—contracting—the volume of money in circulation, so that 50 cents will buy as much as a dollar would (and that is "hard pan," "specie basis," resumption argument,) why should I complain that my wages are reduced from $1 to 50 cents, per day? If there is no just cause of complaint, why complain if the volume of money is reduced, contracted, so that 25 cents will buy as much as 50 cents? Or to 12 1.2 cents per day, it buying as much in the market as the 25 cents formerly did?

Let us look at this matter a little: Why, if it makes no difference, should any one complain at having free coinage of silver, thus increasing the volume of money in circulation until $2 will buy no more than $1 formerly? Or to $4 per day for the ordinary wage-worker, it buying no more, because of its cheapness (?), than the §1 or §2 at the former status of money matters? If sauce for the goose should be sometimes sauce for the gander—the rule working both ways occasionally—who should object?

THE BLACK BRUTES
Who Tried to Kill the Operator at Chillicothe are Captured.
An Attempt Made to Lynch Them.
Yesterday the BAZOO gave an account of the attempt, by some negroes at Chillicothe, a town on the H. & St. Joe, to murder the telegraph operator, a young man by the name of Fred Tucker, at an early hour.

The assault was a cold-blooded, premeditated attempt at as foul a murder as was ever conceived, utterly dastardly in its conception.

Thanks to poor marksmanship, the unsuspecting young man was not killed, though he received an ugly wound in his right cheek, and one in the thumb of his right hand.

THE REPORT OF SHOTS
at once brought quite a crowd to the depot, before whose appearance the negros fled. A party large at once formed and searched the country for the would-be assassins. Late in the afternoon one of the men was captured near Meadville by George Graham and Policeman Tom Anderson, of Chillicothe, who took their prisoner back with them. Tucker identified the man as one of the crowd who made the attack. Still later in the evening a second member of the murderous gang was captured and taken back to the scene of attack. He, too, was recognized, and was sent to join his companion in the jail. The news of the capture of the men increased the excitement in the town, and threats of lynching
and it is hardly possible that any of the men engaged in the attack could be recognized.

Next morning the excitement had, to a considerable extent, died away, and all danger of a lynching picnic is considered past. Tucker, the wounded man, is doing well and will soon be back at his duty.

The conductor on the H. & St. Joe train this morning told a different story of the attack to an Evening Star reporter. He said the man who did the shooting approached the door of the office, and seeing Tacker stretched out upon a table, deliberately fired at him without a word of warning.

A number of negroes tried to rob the H. & St. J. R. R. depot at Chillicothe on Saturday morning, June 11. Two of them made an attack on Fred Tucker assistant telegraph operator, and shot him in the face and hand. The party was frightened off and did not succeed in their attempt at robbery. At one o'clock Monday morning 75 masked men appeared at the jail and demanded the prisoners of sheriff Leeper, but that officer advised them to disperse and let the law take its course. United States Pensions.

The payment of $100,000,000 in pensions during the present fiscal year has seemed an immense burden, but it is said that it will be $50,000,000 greater next year, $100,000,000 the following year, and at least $75,000,000 the year after that. The annual appropriation for pensions should then be not more than $50,000,000, although that sum will seem large to pay at the end of nearly a quarter of a century from the war. The payment of pensions to disabled soldiers and sailors, is most cheerfully made, but the knowledge that a large per cent of the pension money goes into the hands of persons whose names have found a place on the pension list through fraud, excites the righteous indignation of the people.—Exchange.

Deputy Sheriff, Will Leeper, Shoots the Wrong Man.
It having been reported that Alex Murray, the colored desperado, who escaped from the penitentiary, had been seen in the vicinity of the depot, Deputies Frank Green and Will Leeper, on Thursday night watched for him at the Hannibal depot. While they were watching, a person, with a veil over his face, emerged from behind some ties near the depot and advanced on to the depot platform. Leeper ordered him to halt, which he did not do, when Leeper fired at him three times with a revolver, one shot taking effect in his abdomen. The person proved to be William Duncan, a young man who resides in this city. Duncan says he, also, was watching for Murray, in company with John Hereford, colored; that he had a shotgun, which he left on the pile of ties and came to the depot platform to watch the crowd as the train came in. He says he did not hear Leeper call halt. The wound proved to be only a flesh wound and at last accounts Duncan was rapidly recovering.

Leeper is exhonerated from blame, as he had been informed that Murray was heavily armad and had declared his intention to kill anyone who should attempt to arrest him and that he had been hiding among the piles of ties.

They Beat the Old Man.

Cameron Vindicator.

Trenton is in a state of great excitement occasioned by the elopement of two prominent young people of that place, Saturday night. The lady in the case is Miss Minnie Hoffman, daughter of one of the wealthiest merchants of Trenton, and the gentleman Prof. DeBeuchel Lew, a prominent musician. It seems that the father of the young lady opposed the match, but this did not deter them from meeting, and fixing up a plan of beating the old man. They left Trenton on the Rock Island train Saturday evening, proceeded to Gallatin, got out a marriage license, were married, boarded the Wabash train and left for St. Louis, where they are now enjoying their honeymoon. After they were married and safe, the following telegram was sent to Trenton: "Both voters. Going to have a good time. Tata."

Richard L. Altbritain, Esq.

The numerous friends of this talented young gentleman will be deeply grieved to learn of his death about 6 o'clock this morning, at the residence of P. H. Minor, Esq. He was a son of the late Jas. Allbritain, and a grand-son of Andrew Craig. These gentlemen were early pioneers of Livingston county, and were long in the very front of our most active, usetul and honored citizens.

Richard was born and raised to manhood in this county. He was a graduate of the Normal School at Kirksville, and for a time taught school—notably, several years in the public schools of Jefferson City. During the intervals of school he read law under the advice and assistance of C. H. Mansur, Esq., of this city, and part of the time in his office. He was possessed of great energy and perseverance, and was talented in a large degree. He was the first young gentleman, under the law as it now exists, to apply to our Supreme Court for an examination, in open court, for license as an attorney, and his examination was one alike worthy of the court and of the candidate. Being admitted to the bar about three years ago, he located at Kansas City, and so great was his industry and his ability that in a twelve months he had gained a standing at that bar that made him self-supporting, and having won the affections of Miss Caddie Bolton, a most estimable young lady of Jefferson City, they were married about two years ago. No young man had a brighter future than Richard; and in his death his wife and relatives, his friends and his country, alike meet with a loss that is irreparable.

Last July, one sultry night, after being very much heated, he sat or stood in a draft, and becoming chilled, the cold settled upon his lungs, and resulted we think, from all we can learn, in a case of galloping consumption, that eventuated in his death.

Brought home, last Thursday night, by his brother William, and accompanied by his faithful and loving wife, he only returned to the scenes of his childhood and the home of his family to rapidly wither and die, like a fallen oak struck by lightning.
His remains were taken on the afternoon passenger, to-day, via Kansas City to Jefferson City, for interment. Richard L. Allbritain's generous qualities and noble nature will long keep his memory green in the minds of his many friends in Livingston county; and whose sympathy, in no unstinted measure, go out to his afflicted wife and relatives.

BODIES RECOVERED.

Chicago, Oct. 26.—The bodies of George H. Murdgens, drowned from a row boat on the 15th instant, and of John Ryan, the varieties and concert saloon manager, reported in these dispatches as missing, were recovered from the lake this afternoon. Ryan, it is believed, committed suicide. Murdgens was clerk for a commercial agency.

ARBESTED FOR MURDER.

St. Louis, Oct. 26.—Antonio Ritta, a Sicilian rag-picker, sixty years old, was arrested to-night charged with killing Valero Robaro, a boy of seven years, who lived next door to Ritta, 320 Almond street. The affair is involved in great mystery, but circumstances indicate that Ritta shot the boy under the belief that he had stolen a pistol from his room.

Shenandoah, Pa., Oct. 26.—This afternoon three brothers, Peter, James and Henry Sheetz, Timothy Reynolds and Robert Hanna were entombed at Packer colliery No. 3, operated by the Lehigh Valley Coal company, by the caving in of dirt. antonio-de-rita-st-louis-1882-11.A2:
SENSATIONS OF TO-DAY
A BOY MURDER IN ST. LOUIS.
A Highly Dramatic Scene in the Discovery of the Murderer—Twin Mysteries—Sudden and Unaccountable Disappearance of two Girls From Chicago and Milwaukee.
the yard in the rear of the old brick row on the south side of Almond, between Third and Fourth streets, was the scene of a mysterious tragedy last evening just after 6 o'clock; and when darkness had just taken the place of daylight, the sound of a pistol shot startled the occupants of the row and brought those who were in out of doors. The first arrivals found Barbato Urgbars, an Italian boy aged 7, prostrated and breathing his last. The bullet had penetrated his heart, causing death instantly. The boy's grandmother started to pick him up, but before she could do so he was dead. The boy had fallen in front of the kitchen door in the rear of 318 Almond street, the house occupied by his parents. Just here there is a passage way that leads from the kitchen to the yard, which is in the rear of a lot of brick sheds. The old lady believed that her grandson's assailant had shot him while he was in the yard, for he had gone there to wash his hands at the hydrant, which is used for that purpose by all who live in the row. The old woman ran into the yard. The first person she saw sitting there was Antonia Deritta, an Italian rag-picker. He was a few feet from the hydrant. His wife sat upon her door-step, and did not seem the least disconcerted; the grandmother rushed up to Deritta and denounced him as the murderer of the child. When he attempted to move away she seized him and called aloud to the neighbors to assist her in making him a prisoner. She says he drew a knife and struck at her, at the same moment threatening to kill her if she did not release him. She then let go of the man, but before he could leave the yard a crowd of excited Italians—men and women—surrounded him. Deritta crossed himself as the people manifested their indignation, and, looking meek as a lamb, called upon heaven to witness his innocence. His wife, a resident of Almond street for years, went to her husband's rescue. She also crossed herself and vowed that Deritta was innocent of the killing. They said a revolver had been stolen from them that morning, and claimed that the dead boy was the thief, and that his death was the accidental discharge of the weapon. The bystanders looked around for other witnesses. There was no one in the yard at the time of the shooting except Derrita and wife, the two latter claimed, but while the excitement was at its height some one discovered that Angelo Urgbaro, a five-year-old brother of the deceased, was standing near Deritta when the shot was fired. He was questioned, and said that the shooting was done by Deritta. The child told how Deritta had drawn his revolver; how he had fired, and how, following the report, Barbara had run around into the passageway and fallen. This evidence made the blood of the dead child's parents boil, and their cries aroused the sympathy of other residents of the row. There were all manner of threats, and a majority of the men in the crowd seemed eager to take Deritta and lynch him. When the excitement was at fever heat police officer Hutton ran into the yard. He found Deritta at the mercy of a number of men and women who seemed to be doing their best to tear him to pieces. Hutton ordered the crowd back, and so surprised were they at his sudden appearance that they released their prisoner. The officer then thrust him into Almond street with the crowd close at their heels. In less than five minutes a thousand or more men, women and children gathered, and it looked as though mob law was to prevail, for hundreds of excited Italians were in the throng, and all were shouting for Deritta's blood. At the southeast corner of Fourth and Almond streets there is a police patrol alarm box. Hutton opened the door, pushed his prisoner into the box, pulled the hook, then closed the door and locked it. This prompt action saved Deritta's life, for before the crowd had a chance to surround the box or get tools with which to break it open, the patrol wagon arrived and the prisoner was taken to the Chestnut Street Station. The body of the murdered child was taken to the morgue.

CRIMES AND CASUALTIES.
Explosion of a Tag Boiler on Lake Michigan—Fatal Railroad Accidents—Accidentally Poisoned—Train Wreckers at Work—Fatal Affrays.
TUG EXPLOSION.

RACINE, Wis., Oct. 28.—The tug Wetzel blew up this morning 12 miles north of this city while racing with the tug Sill for a tow. The vessel was completely demolished. F. F. Lovell, captain and owner, Wm. Kelly of Chicago, engineer, and Pat White, of Racine, were killed. The explosion was so powerful, that none of the bodies have been found.

POISONED PANCAKES.

BUFFALO, Oct 28.—Mrs. Regar, one the family poisoned by eating pancakes yesterday, has died since. The father and another child are very sick.

SPLIT HIS HEAD OPEN.

AKRON, O., Oct. 28.—Last night seven miles north of here, Thos. Brock and one Detro, colored, had a quarrel at a dance and Brock split Detro's head open with an axe, killing him instantly. Brock has surrendered.

HELD FOR MURDER.

St. Louis, Oct. 28.—The coroner's jury that sat in inquest on the body of the little Italian boy Vevenade Aubno, who was shot night before last, returned a verdict that the child was killed by Antonio De Ritta, the old Sicilian who was arrested for the act. Ritta will be held for murder.

RAILROAD ACCIDENT.

New Albany, Ind., Oct. 28.—The St. Louis air line last night, met with its first serious accident since it has been running through trains. The St. Louis express, which left here at 8:20 last night, was thrown from the track at Boston station, Crawford county, Ind., forty-eight miles west of New Albany. The fireman, John McSwain, of Louisville, Ky., was killed and the passengers shaken up. The accident occurred about 11 o'clock, and was caused by a misplaced switch. The switch lock had been tampered with, and was found broken, evidently by outside parties. The train was running slowly at the time; consequently only the engine and combination car left the track. The engine was ditched and turned over. McSwain was caught under the machine and instantly killed. Several passengers were bruised a little, but only one was injured seriously. The remains of the fireman were taken to Evansville.

BENNETT'S ARREST.

Chicago, Oct. 28.—Some days ago a young man named Henry D. Bennett, collection clerk for a Minneapolis agricultural implement house, was arrested here for appropriating checks and drafts belonging to his employers. He has been secretly kept since then. It is now claimed that he gained access to money letters of other firms and that he had accomplices in Chicago who passed the checks for him here, while he did the like for them in Minneapolis. Who these accomplices were has not transpired.

ANOTHER DEATH.

North Adams, Mass., Oct. 28.—Wm. McDonald, another victim of the recent railroad casualty, died this morning. This is the seventh death since Saturday.

KILLED BY A BLAST.

Silverton, Col., Oct. 28.—Yesterday the bodies of Homer Stewart and Jas. Sullivan were found terribly mangled in the tunnel of the Lancaster mine. Two days ago they went to the mine to do assessment work. It is thought they were killed by a premature blast.

HELD FOR CARELESSNESS.

PHILADELPHIA, Oct. 28.—Sharpenburg and Keever, who superintended the display of fireworks Tuesday night when the explosion occurred by which eight persons were killed, have been held to await the action of the district attorney.

GOT USED TO IT.

PALESTINE, Ind., Oct. 28.—The saloon occupied by Joe Rhinehart was blown up last night for the fourth time by dynamite. The explosion was terrific, and shattered several buildings adjoining. No one hurt. No clue to the perpetrators. No excitement, as the people have got used to it.

POISONED.

SHREVEFORT, Oct. 28.—Eight colored people were poisoned to-day on Wallace plantation, Cossier Parish, by mistaking arsenic for yeast powder and using it in their bread.

BOLD BURGLARY.

WEST BROOKFIELD, Mass., Oct. 28.—Clark's drug store, Blair's block, was broken into last night, the safe blown open and $150 taken. While at their work the robbers were surprised by clerk John McEwer, but got outside the door. In the pursuit pistols were used and McEwer received a wound in the abdomen. The burglars took the early outbound train, and when it reached Charlton compelled the train hands to stop the train and they escaped.

ATTEMPT AT KIDNAPPING.

CLEVELAND, Oct. 28.—A bold attempt at kidnapping was made to-day on Superior street during the busiest part of the day. A lady, accompanied by a five-year-old child, was looking at the display of goods in a store window when a middle-aged woman, unobserved by the mother, threw the skirt of a waterproof she wore around the child, picked it up, stifling the cries, and hurried into a passing street car. The mother did not miss the little one for some moments, and discovered her loss just in time to look eagerly about, see the strange woman enter the car with the child and to rescue it, but was too excited to take measures for the arrest of the kidnapper, who escaped.

EDITOR FREE PRESS: A mysterious and apparently cold blooded murder took place at an early hour this morning at No. 318, Almond steeet. The victim being a Sicilian boy named Val Robaro. The lad was shot down in the presence of a younger brother and died in his mother's arms shortly afterwards, and with his dying breath accused an old man named Darita of doing the shooting, and gave as a probable reason for the deed, some trivial provocation. Darita and his wife are both locked up, charged with murder.

The "testimonial benefit" in behalf of the children of the late Col. A. W. Slayback, ook place at the Olympic Theatre yesterday. Never before in the history of St. Louis was ever witnessed such an assemblage of representative citizens at a place of amusement. They came with one thought and purpose, to help the orphaned children of a man so generally respected and loved. The combined orchestras of Grand Opera House and the Olympic Theatre performed for the occasion, and the programe opened with the singing of Gounod's "Ave Maria" by Miss Fritch, (violin, piano and organ accompaniment,) and the vast throng stood spell bound at the sweetness of this initial performance. There came a recitation by Mr. Pope, and finally the tragedy of "Julius Caesar," by the John McCullough troupe, with McCullough as Brutus. A perfect storm of applause greeted the tragedian, whose splendid acting and historic fame is only equaled by his princely generosity to the needy and deserving. McCullough himself tendered this "benefit" to the stricken family, with a $1000 thrown in, and your readers may imagine the interest manifested by the citizens in response to Mr. McCullough, when I say that seats sold at from one thousand dollars to two hundred dollars a piece, and many ladies and gentlemen yesterday were offering one and two hundred dollars for a single seat, any where in the house; but at the opening of the performance not even standing room could be purchased at any price.

The fall elections in the city are approaching, and the conflict between rival candidates and opposing political factions is bitter and unrelenting, and the scences at our "ward meetings" are disorderly and often disgraceful.

The mamouth paper warehouse of Holms & Co., of this city, heretofore declared unsafe, fell with a fearful crash into a heap this morning, an extensive conflagration ensued, and the ruins are still conflagration fiercely as I write this letter. It is not positively known if any lives were lost.

CARL SMYTHE.

DENVER (Col.) March 6th —The Republic.
A Jail Attacked and Prisoners Shot.
DENVER (Col.), March 6th. — The Republican's special says: Arnold Howard and Frank Young, charged with cattle-stealing, were arrested Thursday and placed in jail at Del Norte. The next day an attempt was made to break jail, but was prevented. Saturday night 100 mounted man, said to be stock men from the Rio Grande and San Luis valleys, rode down on the guards, ordered them to throw up their hand and commenced firing in every direction. When the jail was broken the prisoners attempted to escape. Young was mortally wounded and Howard was killed outright. The body of the latter was thrown into the river. The windows of the jail were riddled with bullets. Howard has been arrested twelve times on a charge of cattle stealing, and in every instance was cleared.

Municipal Elections.
PORTLAND (Me.), March 6th. — The vote for Mayor of the city resulted in no choice. Libby (Rep.) 2,719; Deering (Citizens' and Democrat.) 2,259; Littlefield (Temperance), 483; scattering, 47. The Republicans elect all the School Committees, five Aldermen and fourteen Councilmen. The Democrats elect one Alderman and six Councilmen. No election for one Alderman and one Councilman.

Hollowell elects James H. Leigh (Rep.) Mayor by 252 majority; also the straight Republican ticket in every ward. This result has not been attained in that city for many years.

David Farrar (Rep.) is elected Mayor of Lewiston over Garcelon (Fusion) by a vote of 1,348 to 900. The Republicans elect five Aldermen and the Democrats elect two. In Auburn Gao, S. Woodman (Rep.) is elected Mayor by a small majority.

MOBILE (Ala.), March 6th. — At the municipal election to-day the straight Democratic ticket was successful—electing the Mayor, Municipal Board and probably Tax Collector.

WHISKEY THE CAUSE OF IT.

St. Louis, March 7.—Santa Fe special: Governor Sheldon received news from Toos Pueblo yesterday, which substantiated is serious. It is to the effect that four days ago some Toos Pueblos became drunk. They were arrested and placed in jail. They escaped and deputy Sheriff Myers and Martinez started to Pueblo to re-arrest them. They and their posse were met by fifty-nine armed Pueblo Indians and a fight ensued, in which Deputy Sheriff Myers was killed and Deputy Sheriff Martinez mortally wounded. The murderers are not yet captured. The Toos Pueblos is one of the richest and largest tribes in the territory and heretofore the best of feeling has existed between the Pueblos and the surrounding Mexican towns. Of late too much whiskey traffic has been going on, which the United States authorities should stop. Gov. Sheldon has sent to Toos for latest information and the news is hourly expected.

Arkadelphia, Ark., March 7—In a shooting affray yesterday one negro was killed and two mortally hurt.

MURDER WITHOUT CAUSE.

A QUARRELSOME drunkard named John Davidson killed his aged mother, in Philadelphia, Pa., May 4. There had been an altercation over some money matters, during which pans and chairs were thrown about the rooms, and John seized a hatchet and struck his mother a savage blow on the top of the head. This he repeated time after time, until the woman's brains were scattered on the floor, when the neighbors, startled by the tumult, rushed in.

PROHIBITION is enforced with dynamite in Cedarville, Ohio. One end of C. Sweeney's saloon, near the railway, was blown out on the 4th, the owner, his wife, and children being thrown from bed to the floor. An attempt was made to destroy Caldwell's drug store, but the charge did not explode.

Mrs. Newton, of Louisville, Ky., apprehensive that the father of her adopted son would take him from her, gave the little fellow a dose of morphine, on the 3d, wrote a note of explanation, and then drugged herself. The boy died. Mrs. Newton will probably recover.

HOWARD, the Del Norte horse and cattle thief, who escaped from a mob who took him out of jail to hang him, was surprised on a ranch near Pueblo, Colo., on the 6th, and captured after a desperate resistance.

SEVERAL blocks of buildings were buryed at Racine, Wis., the other morning. The loss was over half a million.

The Canadian banks were forbidden last July to issue any more $4 bills, but by some queer freak the public demands them, and the Dominion Government will hereafter issue bills or that denomination. —Chicago Herald.

At a recent dinner party in New York the colored servants were dressed in the style of a century ago, and looked as if they had stepped out of pictures of Mount Vernon in the good old days when George Washington was lord of the manor.

The disposition of colored people to visit and console sick friends is illustrated in a case in Georgia. A colored woman was attacked by colic. About one hundred of her sympathizing friends collected around her bedside. The floors gave way and the house was wrecked. —N. Y. Herald.

Our fashionables will be dismayed to learn that the most polished nation in the world has decided it is not now "the thing" to wear a watch chain in view. What in the world is to become of the massive plated chain cables to which our watches are suspended? —Detroit Free Press.

In Duval County, Florida, dwells a polygamist with three wives. A negro deemed it a duty to prosecute him, and, after gathering the requisite proof, started for the Court House to make a complaint. He had gone only a few miles when the polygamous husband overtook and shot him. —Chicago News.

A Brooklyn man gets $500 from a dentist who broke one of his teeth and let the fragment fall into the windpipe, where it stuck. The patient was under the influence of gas at the time, didn't know what had happened, was doctored for bronchitis, and only sued the dentist after coughing up the ivory at the end of a long sickness.

Now if you'd come a week ago I could have taken you to three lynchings and a dance, but just now there isn't much sport on hand. However, if you like, we'll go down to the saloon and start a fight. —Dr. Hammond says that a great many persons are afflicted with the "reasoning mania." We are compelled to add to this statement our conviction that the number, large as it is, bears a very small proportion to the countless hosts who have an unreasoning mania. Physical science is certainly very trying and very exasperating. If one's brains are as wet and soggy as the muck of a marsh he is called an idiot; if one's brain is so active that it dives into everybody's affairs, peers through the keyhole of every chamber and pries into every possible secret, he has a reasoning mania; and if he has just intellect enough to mind his own business, and nothing more—well, the number of the latter is so extremely small that, as yet, science has not classified them.—N. Y. Sun.

geo-ellis-catlettsburg-1882-01-03.A1:
HORRIBLE MURDER.
Arrest and Confession of the Murderers.
Advices from Ashland, Ky., state that the murderers of the Gibbons children have been arrested on the confesssion of one of them. All live in Ashland, and two of them are married men. They are in the Cattleburg jail. Lynching is expected tonight.

A special from Ashland, Ky.. says: The three men arrested for the Gibbons murder are Wm. Neal, Ellis Craft and Geo. Ellis, all white. Ellis says Craft and Neal awakened him on the night of the murder and urged him to go with them to the Gibbons house. He went reluctantly. They entered by a window, and Neal and Craft outraged the two girls. Emma Thomas recognized Neal and said she would tell her mother. Robert, the boy, was then about to give an alarm when Craft struck him on the head with an axe, killing him instantly. Craft then told Fanny her time to die had come, and amid viteous cries of the child for mercy, he struck her on the head and killed her instantly. Neal then killed Emma Thomas in the same way. Craft and Neal at first denied Ellis' story, but Neal confessed this afternoon and both he and Ellis waived an examination. Craft will have a hearing Thursday. Ellis and Neal are married; Craft is single. They were all present when Gibbon's residence was burned and one of them drove the hearse at the funeral and another was a pall bearer. Crowds have been gathering all day at Cattlesburg and threats of lynching are common.

THE WEST.
Kentucky.
Determined Vigilantes—A Sheriff's Race for Life With His Prisoners.

CATLETTSBUG, Jan. 5.—The three men who murdered two girls after outraging them and also murdered a brother of one of the girls to prevent him raising an alarm, afterwards firing the house, during the absence of the father of two of the victims, Mr. Gibson, at Ashland, were secretly moved from jail by the sheriff this afternoon to save them from being lynched by the crowd that had organized for the purpose. The sheriff took the prisoners in a close cab aboard a ferryboat bound for Ohio. The vigilantes learning of this chartered the steamboat Mountain Girl and boarding her went in pursuit. The sheriff, when he learned that he was pursued, headed for down the river and at last accounts it was a race for life.

geo-ellis-catlettsburg-1882-01-03.A10:
THE ASHLAND FIENDS.
A Narrow Escape from the Hands of the Mob.
The Scoundrels Placed on a Steamboat and Started for Maysville-The Mob Take Possession of Another and Pursue.
A LONG AND EXCITING CHASE.
First Dispatch.
sarmo Ky. January 5.
First Dispatch.

CATLETTSBURG, Ky., January 5.—A special says: Judge Brown, fearing the great crowd from Ashland would prevent the hearing of the cases of the Gibbons family murders, ordered the steamer Mountain Girl to get up steam and take the prisoners to Maysville, Ky., for safe keeping. Owing to the difficulty of getting the prisoners on board the sheriff put them on the ferry boat and started down the river. The mob took possession of the steamer Mountain Girl, and started in pursuit. It is thought that the prisoners will not get to Maysville alive.

Second Dispatch.

IRONTON, Ohio. January 5.—The trial at Catlettsburg, of the Ashland murderers, was set for 1 o'clock. Judge Brown, fearing the action of the mob, about 2,000 strong, had the prisoners placed on a ferry boat which transferred them to the Mountain Boy, at the Sheridan's coal works, three miles below Catlettsburg. The mob hearing this, captured the steamer Mountain Girl, and are in hot pursuit. Mountain Boy passed here, ten miles from Catlettsburg, with prisoners, at 2 P. M., the Mountain Girl not here yet.

2:40 P. M.—It is supposed that Mountain Boy will be overtaken before she reaches Maysville, as the Mountain Girl stopped at Ashland, and the mob are now making efforts to secure a train to head off the Mountain Boy at Portsmouth or the nearest port below.

Another Account.

CINCINNATI, January 5.—The Gazette's Ashland, Ky., special says: Judge Brown, upon hearing that a mob was coming from Ashland to lynch the prisoners, issued an order for the removal of the prisoners to the Mason county (Maysville) jail, and Craft having waived an examination he adjourned the Circuit Court till January 16th.

Citizens here are very indignant at Brown. They had gone to protect the prisoners, and the prosecuting committee had asked the Governor for troops to assist in keeping order, and it was in response to this that the troops were started up from Maysville. The citizens sent a committee to Judge Brown to ask him to rescind his order, but he refused.

A dispatch has been sent Senator Moore to get an act passed, to-morrow, appointing a session of the court next Monday for the trial.

VANCEBURG, Ky., January 5.—The steamer Mountain Boy arrived here at 7:30 with the Ashland fiends on board, expecting to reach their destination, the Maysville jail, about midnight.

Sheriff John Kounz left Greenup at six o'clock and embarked on the B. F. Enos for Catlettsburg, arriving there at 10:30, in time to attend the preliminary examination of Ellis Craft. Craft waived an examination.

The excitement was rife, and the rapidly growing crowd threatened violence. Word was received that a train, loaded with lynchers, had started from Ashland, and was expected at any time. Fearing the mob, the Mountain Girl, which was lying at the wharf, was chartered to convey the prisoners to Maysville.

While the Girl was raising steam, the train from Ashland rolled in, with about 500 determined regulators on board. The Sheriff, with a party of ten guards, by an adroit movement, removed the prisoners from the jail to the wharf.

As soon as the crowd beheld the prisoners, they started down the bank with loud yells of indignation, gathering arms and missles ready for an assault. The Sheriff, seeing the mob descending, and the Girl not yet having steam up, boarded the ferry boat with his party, and turned her down stream. The mob took possession of the Mountain Girl, cut her loose and commenced a determined chase.

The Mountain Girl not having sufficient steam pressure, soon fell behind, but in a short time she got in shape and commenced gaining rapidly on the slow ferry, and in a short time the Girl approached so closely that a capture seemed imminent, but fortunately the Mountain Boy, a faster boat than the Girl, approached on the scene, on her regular trip up from Ashland to Louisiana, She was hailed by the Sheriff and pressed into service, and the party rapidly transferred to her. When the transfer had been successfully made, the girl Black with an excited, enraged and howling mob, was right on their heels, and the exciting chase was resumed. But the Boy, flying light, showed her a clean pair of heels.

Near Ashland, the Hudson with the Kentucky militia, was met in mid stream. Capt. A. C. Respess, of the Mason County Guards and twenty-five men were transferred to the Boy and took charge of the prisoners. The pursuing vessel was still in sight, but when they learned was commenced a determined chase.

MAYSVILLE. January 5.—The Ashland murderers arrived here at 10 o'clock tonight, and were safely lodged in jail.

Arrival of the Ashland Prisoners at Maysville.

Capt. A. C. Respess, with a detachment of the Mason County Guards, who left here yesterday morning for Catlettsburg, in obedience to orders from the Governor, arrived here last night, at ten o'clock by the steamer Mountain Boy, having in custody Neal, Craft and Ellis, the men arrested on the charge of having committed the recent horrible murder at Ashland, Ky. Yesterday morning, at Catlettsburg, a mob numbering probably two thousand persons, collected for the avowed purpose of lynching the prisoners, but the sheriff and posse under pretense of arraigning them for their preliminary examination, took them to the court house, and subsequently removed them by a back door to the river where the Mountain Girl was supposed to be in readiness to take them sway, but when the sheriff reached the boat it was found to have only 20 pounds of steam. They were then taken to a a ferryboat, closely followed by the mob, but reached it in advance of them and succeeded in getting away from the landing. The mob seized the Mountain Girl and raising steam by the use of rosin followed in pursuit. Several miles below Catlettsburg the sheriff's party met the Mountain Boy
coming up and transfering the prisoners to her she was turned about and headed down stream, the Mountain Girl still following. Near Riverton the Hudson was met, having the guards on board. They were transferred to the Mountain Boy and the pursuit here ended. The prisoners on their arrival at this place were placed in the jail, which has since been closely guarded by the troops. Capt. Respess, in obedience to orders from Judge George N. Brown, of the sixteenth district, will take the prisoners to Catlettsburg for trial on the 16th inst. The services of the soldiery will probably be needed until the trial is over.

The prisoners are bad looking men and of a brutal type. Neal is about thirty years of age and has been a mill hand at the Northern Iron Works, at Ashland. Craft, who is about the same age, is a farmer by occupation and is considered the shrewdest of the three. Ellis is probably thirty-three years of age and is a laborer. He has confessed to participating in the murder, and claims to have been forced to take the part he did. He has admitted that the Gibbons and Thomas girls were ravished, and that he and his companions were guilty alike. He says also, that he poured coal oil upon the bodies of the girls and the crippled boy preparatory to burning the house. On the way down the river Craft and Neal manifested a stolid indifference to their situation. Ellis, especially while the mob was present exhibited the most object terror. Neal and Craft both claim to be innocent and assert their ability to prove an alibi, at the proper time.

The jail here it is well-known is in such a condition that the safe keeping of prisoners, cannot be assured. It is necessary
a constant guard should be maintained, which the County Judge has ordered to be done.

geo-ellis-catlettsburg-1882-01-03.A13:
THE ASHLAND MURDERERS.
Taken Down the Ohio River in a Steamer Parsued by a Mob.
Yesterday a mob of 450 men started from Ashland, Ky., to go to Cattlettsburgh, some five miles off, for the purpose of lynching Neal, Ellis and Craft, the murderers of Annie Thomas and the Gibbons children. Judge Bowen, becoming uneasy, ordered the prisoners to be taken on board the steamer Mountain Boy, and to be taken to Maysville, from which place a company of soldiers had been ordered.

The sheriff took the prisoners and with difficulty got them on the steamer. Just as she started away the Ashland mob took possession of the steamer Mountain Girl and started in pursuit. At Riverton, about twenty miles below Cattlettsburgh, the steamer Mountain Boy was met by steamer Hudson, which had on board the Maysville guards, numbering 75 muskets. The soldiers were transferred to the Mountain Boy, which then continued down the river, passing Portsmouth at about 5½ p.m. Those on the Mountain Girl, on learning that the murderers were in the care of the militia, wisely gave up the pursuit, and, turning around, started for home. The chase created the greatest excitement all along the river towns, and when the Mountain Boy landed at Portsmouth for coal it was all the troops could do to prevent the people from boarding the steamer at all hazards. It is expected that the prisoners will be safely lodged in Maysville jail soon after midnight.

At Cattlettsburgh there were threats of lynching Judge Strong for sending the prisoners away, and he and Judge Savage kept closely within doors.

A special from Ashland says that the men went to Cattlettsburgh to protect the prisoners and see that they had a fair trial.

Judge Brown had notice of their intention, and hence the bitterest feeling exists against him for sending the prisoners away.

An indignation meeting was held and a resolution adopted, declaring their intention to bring back the prisoners, and pledging their honor to protect them until they have had a fair trial.

A committee was also appointed to wait on Judge Brown and induce him to rescind his order, but the judge refused to do so.

At a later hour a mass meeting was held, and a resolution adopted to appeal to the Legislature for a court to be held on next Monday for the trial of the prisoners. The excitement over the case is intense.
geo-ellis-catlettsburg-1882-01-03.A23:
THE ASHLAND MURDERERS.
Their Approaching Trial-The People Satisfied for the Law to Take Its Course.
CINCINNATI, January 9.—A Catlettsburg, Ky., special says: "The grand jury was impanelled to-day under the special act of the Kentucky Legislature, convening the court to try the Ashland murderers. The foreman of the jury is John Russell, of Ashland, one of the Citizens' Committee formed to arrest and prosecute the perpetrators of this triple crime. The jury is said to be the best ever gathered in Boyd county. It is supposed that they will not report till Tuesday morning. The prisoners, under a guard of State troops, arrive on Wednesday morning. The feeling is that so long as the law takes its regular course towards a speedy trial there will be no danger of interference by the people, but if another attempt is made to remove the prisoners it will be hard to restrain the fury of the people."

CANNON, the delegate in Congress from Utah, is not strengthening his position by his charges that the ministers of the gospel over the country are endeavoring to shape public sentiment against polygamous practices. He will find, if he looks a little closer into the matter, that a very considerable majority of the people of the United States who are not preachers are decidedly opposed to and in favor of legally suppressing polygamy. When the late horrible murder was committed at Ashland, a mob, one of the largest that ever gathered in the state, endeavored to lynch the perpetrators, but the strong arm of the law interfered and they were removed from the impending danger. A WEATHER prophet enlivening New Jersey with his presence, predicts that the present month will be characterized by heavy snows, severe cold and very high winds. girl-rock-creek-washington-1882-07-12.A2:
A HORRIBLE STORY.
A Colored Girl, Eight Years of Age, Outraged by Three White Youths.
One of those horrible outrages upon children which have been so prevalent in the District of Columbia in the past few years, occurred a week ago near the Twentieth street bridge of Rock Creek. On the banks overlooking Rock Creek at this point there resides an honest and hard-working colored man named Louis Martin, his wife and child, Eunice Martin, aged 8 years. The Martins are all respected by their neighbors on account of their frugality and honesty.

One day last week little Eunice, who is a bright, intelligent girl, was sent to the spring, which is distant about 200 yards from the house. The child was gone longer than was her custom, and her parents became alarmed lest she had met with an accident.

Mrs. Martin hastily summoned her husbadd, who was working in the field near by, and told him to repair to the spring at once and ascertain what had become of their little one. Mr. Martin left off work and ran to the spring. He called aloud for his child two or three times, and, failing to get a response, went about investigating. "Eunice, Eunice, Eunice," the poor father cried, but no response did he get.

Finally the neighbors gathered about, and after a long and thorough investigation the little child was found unconscious, lying in a heap of bushes about fifty yards from the spring. She was carried to her home and a doctor summoned, who dressed her wounds. Her body had been torn and mutilated in a frightful manner. When the child regained consciousness she said that she had been met at the sprtgng by three boys, whom she minutely described. From the description furnished by the girl two of the boys must be about 18 years old each, and the other about fifteen.

The case was put into the hands of the police, but as yet the perpetrators of the crime have not been brought to justice. Officer Cole arrested three notorious young characters a few days ago, but the child could not identify them. This case was reported the day after the outrage, and yet only one policeman was put upon the track of the young scoundrels. The question that is being asked is, "Why should not some of our 'flye' detectives be assigned to work up the case?"

TOM LYNCH was arrested last night for disorderly conduct, and a pistol being found concealed upon his person, he was fined for both offenses.

At the meeting of the Georgia Republicans last night no quorum was present, and an adjournment was had, subject to the call of the president.

The infant son of General Babcock died of cholera infantum on Wednesday evening. The many friends of General and Mrs. Babcock deeply grieve with them at their affliction.

The Bashful nine of East Washington and the Record nine of the Government Printing Office will play an interesting game of ball on the old Eagle grounds this evening at 4 o'clock.

A THIEF forced an entrance to F. J. Seybold's residence, 1234 Thirteenth street north-west, yesterday, during the absence of the family, but was scared off without obtaining
MAJOR BROCK has instituted an investigation of the horrible rape perpetrated by white boys upon a little colored girl on Rock Creek, and it is probable that the guilty parties will be arrested to-day.

GEORGE JOHNSON, a large-sized, saffron-hued individual, was charged in the Police Court to-day with having assaulted Laura Noble, a small-sized maiden of a similar color. Johnson was assessed $10 by Judge Snell.

The thief who invaded General Robinson's room last night got off with a $500 Confederate note, a share of landscrip for one hundred acres in West Virginia, a bank account book and an immense number of railroad passes.

The Waverley Baseball Club played a game yesterday afternoon with the Stalwart Baseball Club, and defeated them by a score of 19 to 6. The Waverleys personated the Halfbreeds. The Waverleys go to Harrisburg next month to play the local clubs there.

JOHN MAGWIRE, ESQ., died suddenly of heart disease, after a few day illness, on Wednesday morning, at his rooms, 942 F street northwest, in the 78th year of his age. The remains were sent to St. Louis last night, in care of General E. A. Carr, his son-in-law.

HENRY FLETCHER, a colored man, was charged in the Police Court to-day with invading the sanctity of Annie Miller's ranche in the "Division" and stealing a lamp, some pillows, etc., from Nettle Jackson, one of the frail inmates. Judge Snell sentenced the thief to six months in jail.

The mysterious boatmen who are supposed to have deposited a human body in the Potomac off the Arsenal are still unknown to the police, who have made inquiries and found that several persons saw the mysterious occurrence from different points along the shore, but are all unable to tell where the boat was finally moored.

YESTERDAY afternoon Mr. Thomas Con-olly, the inventor of an improvement on the telephone, living at No. 914 F street, was lighting a pipe which he had recently filled with tobacco, when it suddenly exploded, badly injuring his face and eyes. The supposition is that either a cartridge or some loose gunpowder got into the tobacco and did the mischief.

ABOUT 10 o'clock last night a burglar entered the house of Mr. Armstrong, 1317 F street northwest. Climbing through the second-story back window he entered the room of General Robertson, who was then absent, but being frightened by the cries of a woman, the only occupant of the house at the time, he made his escape. It is not thought that anything was taken.

IN THE CASE of Elizabeth Taylor against Charles Taylor, in which the husband is charged with cruel treatment, the plaintiff this morning procured the leave of Judge Hagner, of the Equity Court, to file an amendment to the bill, and it was filed. The amendment states that in the property from which she was evicted by Allen and Holtzman she has an equitable claim, and she asks that she may have a lien on it for alimony.
girl-rock-creek-washington-1882-07-12.A5:
LIEUTENANT JOHNSON of the County
Precinct submitted a report to Major Brock
LIEUTENANT JOHNSON of the County Precinct submitted a report to Major Brock this morning of the reported rape perpetrated by white boys on a little colored girl, living with her parents near Rock Creek. The report is to the effect that the parents' story of the affair was incorrect, and while the girl was undoubtedly driven from the spring, to which she went for water, and stoned by boys, no indecent assault was perpetrated. What object the girl's parents could have in circulating the story is unexplained. A physician examined the child yesterday, at Lieutenant Johnson's request, and discovered no signs of mutilation or abuse. Four boys have been arrested and taken before the girl for identification, but all have been discharged.

gus-mentzel-raton-1882-06-26.A2:
Bloody Affray—Three Men Killed and Others Wounded—The Murderer Lynched.

RATON, June 26th.—This afternoon Deputy Sheriff Dolman attempted to arrest a gambler named Gus Mentzel. Mentzel fired two shots at Dolman, slightly wounding him; also Charles Fox and Jacob Harris, who were standing near them. Shortly afterwards Dolman made a second attempt to arrest Mentzel at his gambling house. Mentzel again opened fire on the deputy, which resulted in the death of Harry Moulton, Justice of the Peace, Hugh E. Delston, one of the proprietors of the Moulton Hotel, and S. H. Jackson, a saloon-keeper. All three were instantly killed. H. Latimer and Deputy Sheriff Bergan were seriously wounded. Immediately after the killing, Mentzel was seized by the enraged citizens and hanged to the sign of the Raton Bank.

LATER.—Deputy Sheriff Bergan is dying, and the citizens are wild with excitement. It is thought a raid will be made upon the gamblers here to-right.
gus-mentzel-raton-1882-06-26.A3:
THE STRIKES. The Situation To-day at New York and Jersey City. JERSEY CITY, June 27.—The freight handlers, on strike to the number of 1,200, are all united and orderly. There is nothing new in the situation. The truckmen of Matthiessen & Wiechers and Havemeyer & Co., numbering fifty, are on a strike for $13 instead of $12 a week, and for overtime. The coal trimmers of the Morris Canal, between Jersey City and Newark, to the number of 200, have joined the freight-handlers. The trackmen of the Delaware, Lackawanna & Western Road have joined those of the Erie on the strike for $55 instead of $50 per month. NEW YORK, June 27.—The situation of the strike is unchanged. Freight business is blocked. The strikers are sitting on one side of the river front watching Italians and Russian Jews from Castle Garden vainly attempting to handle freight, and policemen are between them and the greenies. One Strike Ended.
POMERoy, O., June 27.—The Crescent rolling mill starts early in July, the proprietor giving the advance until the adoption of a new scale at Pittsburg.

Kentucky's Usual Killings.

FRENCHBURG, Ky., June 27.—Joe Rothwall and Marshal J. B. Day, in fighting out a feud, at first used their fists. Rothwall drew a pistol and shot Day in the leg, whereupon Day bowle-knifed Rothwall to death. Two of Day's brothers shot Rothwell after he was dead.

FRANKFORT, Ky., June 27.—Neal Kelly, a colored desperado, was shot dead by Walter Washington.

James Lamson's sentence to be put to death has been commuted to life imprisonment.

The Malley Murder Trial.

NEW HAVEN, CONN., June 27.—In the Malley trial Coroner C. T. Bollman contradicted Malley's sister's testimony in some important points. Mrs. William E. Hunter, of Southington, testified positively that it was Jennie Cramer and not Maggie Kane who rode the flying-horse. Dr. Moses D. White testified and confirmed the statement that in arsenic eaters the poison would be found in a greater amount in the bones than in other portions of the body.

Indian Agent Llewellyn Killed.

DENVER, COL., June 27.—A gentleman from Socorro, N. M., says Captain Llewelyn, agent of the Mescaleros, was assassinated by renegade Dog Indians.

The Indian Office is not, as yet, in receipt of any information concerning the reported killing of Captain Llewellyn. Commissioner Price says he does not believe the report, though it may be true.

A Mexican Murderer Mobbed.

RATOU, N. M., June 27.—Gus Mentzel, a gambler, while resisting arrest at the Moulton Hotel last evening killed Harry Moulton, a justice of the peace; Hugh Edelston, proprietor of the hotel; S.H. Jackson; also terribly wounding the deputy sheriff, the three men killed being merely bystanders. A mob subsequently lynched Mentzel.

Panic at a Fire.

MANCHESTER, O., June 27.—Eight persons were seriously injured, Mary Sullivan fatally, in a panic caused by the burning of Mrs. Augustine Crosby's boarding-house about midnight. The flames being on the ground floor forty boarders had to escape by the upper windows. The building is damaged $4,000.

Murdered.

RED BANK, N. J., June 27.—The body of John Darmstadt, bridge contractor of the New Jersey Central Road, was found in Shrewsbury River with four knife wounds in his stomach. He was probably murdered. He resided in New York.

DENVER, June 27.—The Tribune's dispatch from Raton, N. M., says that on Monday afternoon Deputy Sheriff Dolmann attempted to arrest a gambler named Gus Mentzel. Mentzel fired two shots at Dolmann, slightly wounding him, also Chas. Fox and Jacob Harris, who were standing near them. Shortly afterward Dolmann made a second attempt to arrest Mentzel at his gambling house. Mentzel again opened fire on the Deputy, which resulted in the death of Harry Houlton, Justice of the Peace, and Hugh Edelston, one of the proprietors of the Moulton Hotel, and S. H. Jackson, a saloon keeper. All three were instantly killed. H. Latimer and Deputy Sheriff Bergan were seriously wounded. Immediately after the killing Mentzel was seized by the enraged citizens and hanged to a sign over the Raton Bank.

[LATER.]

Deputy Sheriff Bergan is dying and the citizens are wild with excitement. It is thought a raid will be made upon the gamblers to-night.
gus-mentzel-raton-1882-06-26.A18:
Bad Place for Gamblers.
RATON, N. M., June 28.—After the lynching of Gus. Mentzel, the gambler who killed four men, citizens took his partner, C. D. R. Bradley, and hung him also.
gus-mentzel-raton-1882-06-26.A23:
LATE NEWS ITEMS.
The bill to amend the act donating land to States which may provide agricultural colleges passed the Senate on the 27th. The bill to reduce internal taxes passed the House—127 to 80.

It is said that the captain of the United States steamer Galena has served notice on all American residents in Alexandria that his vessel is ready to receive them, and they will remain in Egypt at their own risk.

Five thousand Knights of Labor paraded the streets of Rochester, N. Y., June 26, and then held a mass-meeting to take action on the New York penal code. A number of speakers addressed the meeting. Fully 25,000 people were in attendance.

Storm notes from Kansas, Nebraska, and Iowa swell the list of casualties.

G. H. Shewey, of Hillsdale, Mich., Deputy Collector of Internal Revenue, shot himself, June 26, the bullet taking effect in his head behind the ear. He died in his barn a short time after. His mind had been affected for some weeks.

While R. H. Hutter was taking a walk with his wife in Las Vegas, N. Mex., the other evening, an Indian desperado named Francisco Tajoya threw a lariat around his neck, and, putting spurs to his horse, dragged the man over the rock street for 100 yards or more. About 100 yards from the spot where he was lassoed, a bystander, with sudden impulse, pulled a revolver and shot at the flying Indian, who then cut the lariat near the pommel of his saddle. Hutter was terribly bruised and mangled, his long beard being entirely pulled out. The Indian was chased, captured, and lodged in jail. On the 26th a party of citizens took him out and hanged him to a telegraph pole.

At Frenchburg, Menifee County, Ky., the other day, Joe, Sam and William Rothwell, three young men, attempted to revenge upon James B. Day, the Town Marshal, the arrest of a friend named Poore. In the melee which ensued Day and Joe Rothwell were killed.

FIRE in a boarding-house at Manchester, N. H., on the 26th, forced Mary Sullivan, Ellen Ford, Harry Jennings, Margaret McNamara, Eugene Sullivan, Patrick McNamara, Paul Edame, Alice Welch and Michael Marr to jump from the windows, all of whom were badly hurt.

At Raton, N. M., June 26, an attempt by a deputy sheriff to arrest a gambler named Gus Mentzell was followed by a melee, in which Henry Moulton, a Justice of the Peace, Hugh Edelston, one of the proprietors of the Moulton Hotel, and S. H. Jackson, a saloon-keeper, were killed. Immediately after the killing Mentzell was seized by the enraged citizens and hanged to a sign over the Third National Bank.

horn-le-sueur-county-1882-05.A2: The Le Sueur county court disposed of the ravisher Horn in a prompt and expeditious manner. He was indicted on Wednesday, put on trial Thursday morning and in the afternoon Judge McDonald sentenced him to a life-sojourn at Stillwater. Before the court met, an incipient attempt was made to lynch Horn, but failed on account of one of the lynching parties not coming to time.

j-b-lindsey-james-bayou-1882-12-25.A2:
LATEST TELEGRAMS
Crime.
Columbus, Ga., 26.—On Christmas day a difficulty occurred at Troy, Alabama, in which George Folwar was shot dead by Frank Holloway. Several shots were fired by both parties, but only one took effect. The difficulty grew out of an old feud. Both parties are well known business men.

Lon Vinsen was assassinated in Browneville, Alabama, on Monday night.

Frankfort, Iowa, 26.—Officer Laughlin and Geo. Postwood had a difficulty at Lawrenceburg on Saturday night. They took each other by the lappel of the coat, and each shot the other in the breast. Laughlin was killed outright; Postwood died to-day.

Merriton, Ont., 26.—Bessie Bye, aged 15 years, and a sister aged 10, were drowned. The younger attempted to rescue the older, who had broken through the ice whilst skating on the canal.

New Orleans, 24.—At Gill's enterprise, last night, John Booth shot four men, two seriously. Booth escaped. Boston Byron Kimball, stock broker, cut his throat this evening. There is little prospect of his recovery. A letter from a customer was found on his person asking for money invested in cotton speculation.

Meriden, Conn., 26.—An attempt was made to wreck an accommodation train from New York, near this city, by a tie placed on the track. It flew up under the forward truck of the locomotive and brought the train to a stand still, but without damage. Not far behind came the limited express for Boston, the fastest train on the road; it was not more than a train's length from the accommodation train when it stopped with abruptness that almost threw the passengers out of their seats.

Little Rock, 26.—Col. John Rich, an influential citizen, was mentally wounded near McAlmont in an affray with Frank Shayer.

Louisville, 25.—The council, tonight, formally impeached City Auditor Phil Hinkle and Assistant Fire Chief, George W. Levi, city hall officials under indictment for fraud in the assessor's and collector's office.

Cairo, Ill., 26.—J. B. Lindsley was shot dead yesterday, at James' Bayou, Mo. When the steamer Tyler left his murderer was in the hands of the mob and lynching was expected.

Kansas City, 26.—Ayres, arrested on the charge of the murder of Jacob Blibe, musician, yesterday, was sent to jail. The general opinion is that Blibe died by his own hand. There is some mystery about the case, however.

Arkadelphia, Ark., 26.—Lou T. Kretzschmer, secretary of the state senate two years ago, suicided by shooting, at Vernor Station, on Sunday.

Charley Branch (Negro), ravished and murdered a colored girl 9 years old. He was arrested; there are threats of lynching.

Packardville, Mass., 26.—Meriam A Montgomery, 28 years old, shot his two little children this morning, instantly killing George, 6 years, and probably fatally wounding Eva, 4 years. Montgomery and wife separated some months since. She lived with her father. Montgomery visited her family on Saturday and stayed till to-day. Upon her refusal this morning to return to his house, he went out to where the children were playing and then tried to shoot his wife. Her father was overpowered and kept in the house. The sheriff took him to Northampton. He pleaded not guilty when jailed. He says he doesn't remember committed the crime. The whole family came from the west in the spring. Little is known of them.

No marks of violence were visible on his person, while Nutt had cuts and bruises on his face and arms. It is quietly hinted that the citizens are taking the law into their own hands.

St. Louis, 26.—Muskogee, Indian Territory, special: The first open hostilities of the Creek Indian war, occurred on Sunday, fifteen miles from Okmuljee. A band of Checotes men, under Jim Larney, going west, were attached by some 200 of Spiechees partisans, under Commank Mekarochee. The fight raged for an hour when the Checotes men fell back, but kept up a running fight for ten miles. Bob Carr, Dave Barrett and wife, and a man named Walsh, are reported killed. j-b-lindsey-james-bayou-1882-12-25.A3:
TERRIBLE TRAGEDIES, Principally in the South--A Bloody Record of Dark Deeds. Shooting, Stabbing, and Other Modes of Ending Life. Assasination by Unknown Parties--Escaping Murderers. The Usual Homicides in the State of Kentucky-A Policeman Killed.
SAN FRANCISCO, Dec. 26.—A special dispatch to the Tucson Citizen dated Globe says: Yesterday morning, in a saloon at Pioneer, William Hartley stepped to the bar to take a drink when Thomas Kerr, without provocation, knocked him down. Kerr then drew a pistol, and saying, "Young fellow, now I've got you," placed the muzzle to Hartley's breast and fired, killing him instantly. Kerr was disarmed, and a jury of twelve men held an informal trial. He asked for an hour's time to arrange his business. He sat down and with perfect coolness wrote to his mother at Lexington, Ill., requested that all his effects be given to her, and then called for several drinks. The citizens then took him out to a sycamore tree. He made a few remarks, confessing the killing of several men. He was drawn up at once and let down again, then asked permission to take off his boots, saying he did not want to "die with his boots on." This request was granted, and he was swung up. The body was cut down this morning.

PETERSBURG, VA., Dec. 26.—Particulars of a horible double tragedy enacted late Saturday night in Prince George county have just been received here. It appears that Samuel Rives, who is highly connected, became involved in a quarrel with his cousin, William Rives, when a colored man named Parker, endeavored to restore peace between the parties, which so enraged Samuel Rives that he shot the negro through the lungs, killing him instantly. Rives then shot himself, blowing his whole head off. The murderer and suicide was a nephew of Dr. George Rives, and an ex-member of the Virginia legislature.

CHICAGO, ILL., Dec. 26.—About midnight last night, in one of the worst sections of this city, Jennie Griffen, a drunken old vagabond, was celebrating Christmas at home with much clatter and gin. Being interrupted by some young hoodlums, she stabbed one of them, John Mangin, in the shoulder, severing an artery and causing speedy death. She was arrested.

COLUMBUS, GA., Dec. 26.—On Monday afternoon a difficulty occurred at Troy, Ala., in which George Folmar shot and killed Frank Holliway. Several shots were fired by both parties, but only one took effect. The difficulty grew out of an old feud. Both parties are well known business men, and the tragedy has created considerable excitement.

Lon Vinson was assassinated on Monday night by an unknown party.

ARKADELPHIA, ARK., Dec. 26.—Lou T. Kretchmer, secretary of the senate two years ago, and widely known in the state, committed suicide to-day by shooting himself in the head at Varnor station. Sunday a negro named Charles Branch murdered a colored girl 9 years old. He was arrested to-day. Intense excitement exists, and there are threats of hanging by the mob.

NEW ORLEANS, Dec. 26.—The Times-Democrat's Lake Charles special says at Gill's Enterprise last night John Booth shot four men. Two were seriously wounded. Booth escaped, but efforts are being made to capture him.

Last night Robert Waller, while intoxicated, was run over and killed by a passenger train near Lake Charles.

SAVANNAH, GA., Dec. 26.—A special dispatch to the News from Way Cross, Ga., says that William H. Otten, colored, while under the influence of liquor, quarreled with Joe Styles, who thereupon cut Otten's throat and escaped arrest; and that Mollie Baker, also colored, was deliberately shot and seriously wounded by William Davis, colored, while walking on the railway. Davis was arrested.

DUPONT, GA., Dec. 26.—On Saturday night Dennis Clayton, colored, and Fred. Mathos, white, quarreled. They parted and Mathos purchased a knife, and, returning, gashed Clayton's face in a horrible manner.

St. Louis, Dec. 26.—Charles Gilman, a hard character, living at McLeansboro', Ill., shot and killed Addison Sanders yesterday. The shooting is said to have been entirely unprovoked. Gilman was locked up.

FRANKFORT, Ky., Dec. 26.—Town officer Laughlin and George Portwood had a quarrel in Lawrenceburg, Anderson county, last Saturday night, when each shot the other in the breast. Laughlin died at once and Portwood expired to-day.

GALVESTON, TEXAS, Dec. 26.—The News Denison special says: "Yesterday Policeman McCarthy was summoned to arrest a section man named Ellis, who was flourishing a pistol and threatening to shoot. When McCarthy arrested Ellis, the latter ordered him to throw up his hands, and upon his refusing shot him dead. Ellis escaped.

CAIRO, ILL., Dec. 26.—J.B.Lindsley was shot dead yesterday at James Bayou, Mo. When the steamer Tyler left there his murderer was in the hands of a mob and lynching was expected.

LITTLE ROCK, ARK., Dec. 26.—Col. John Rich, an influential citizen of this county, was mortally wounded to-day near McAlmont in an affray with Frank Shaver.

PETERSBURG, Va., December 26.—Samuel Rives became involved in a quarrel with his cousin, Wm. Rives, when a colored man named Parker endeavored to restore peace, which so enraged the former that he shot the negro and then shot himself, blowing his head off.

All Quiet at Opsleka.

All Quiet at Opelka.
Special Dispatch to The BER

Montgomery, Ala., December 26—All quiet at Opelka. The shoriff has a force sufficient to maintain order and sustain the commissioners.

A Stolen "Stake"
Special Dispatch to The BER.

Chicago, December 26.—Thomas Hughes was before Justice Scully this morning, charged with stealing $600 in gold from George Getwood. The pair came to the city together from Omaha on Saturday, and took a room together at the Eagle hotel. Getwood says he woke up late Saturday night and found Hughes bending over his bed. He thought nothing of it at the time, but next morning found his money had been taken from under his pillow. No trace of the missing gold has been found. The case was continued till to-morrow.

A Father's Bloody Deed.
Special Dispatch to The BER.

Springfield, Mass., December 26.—Merriam A. Montgomery, about 28 years old, shot his two little children at Packardville, near Amherst, this morning, instantly killing George, 6 years old, and probably fatally wounding Eva, 4 years old. Montgomery had not lived with his wife for eight months, leaving her through jealousy, and she made her home with her father, Horatio Marsh, a farmer. Mrs. Montgomery visited her family Saturday and stayed till to-day. This morning he asked his wife if she would live with him and she refused. He immediately went out to where the children were playing and shot them. He then tried to shoot his wife and her father, but was overpowered by the latter and kept in the house till the sheriff came. He was taken to Northampton, pleaded not guilty and was sent to jail.

Blits's Blow Out.
Special Dispatch to The BER.

KANSAS CITY, December 26.—A warrant was sworn out to-day charging Addie Ayres with the murder of Jacob Blitz, musician, yesterday morning. The defendant was sent to jail to await a hearing, which will be given on Friday. The general opinion is that Blitz died by his own hand.

Speedy Justice
Special Dispatch to The Bess.

CINCINNATI, December 26.—The Commercial's, Cairo, (Ills.) special says: J. B Lindsey was shot dead yesterday at James Bayou, Mo. When the steamer Tyler left, his murderer was in the hands of a mob, and lynching was expected.

Cremated While Drunk.
Special Dispatch to The Bess.

SAN FRANCISCO, December 26.—Portland (Oregon) dispatch says: Last night a dwelling house near Co-

wallis, Benton county, was destroyed by fire. Two young men were bured to a crisp and a third so badly injured that he is not expected to recover. The parties went to bed drunk, leaving a fire burning, which communicated to the building. The others inmates escaped.

Dukes-Nutt.

PITTSBURG. December 26.—A dispatch from Uniontown says intense feeling against Dakes has developed within the past twenty-four hours. It has been pretty clearly shown that he had been begging off for some time and had proposed meeting at a hotel Sunday for a settlement of the difficulty. No marks of violence are visible on his person, while Nutt has cuts and bruises on his face and arms. It is quietly hinted that there is a possibility of the citizens taking the law into their own hands.

The Swelling Reduced.
Special Dispatch to THE BER.

LITTLE ROCK, December 26.—An Arkadelphia special to the Gazette says: The son of T. Kretzshmer, secretary of the state senate two years ago, and widely known throughout the state, suicided by shooting himself in the head to-day.

An Actress Shot in the Ear.
Special Dispatch to THE BER.

ROCHESTER, December 26.—Lillian Spencer was shot and severely wounded by one of her company at the Academy of Music to-night. It took place at the close of the first act, called "Article 47," when Duhamel shoots Clara. A. H. Forrest played Duhamel, and he fired a blank cartridge at too close proximity to Miss Spencer. She received the charge in the ear. The wound is not serious.
