Daily Leader. THURSDAY. DECEMBER 28, 1882. TELEGRAPHIC NEWS IN BRIEF.
Chicago is discussing elevated railroad schemes.

Many localities in the east are forming Blaine clubs.

Chicago has become the fifth largest port of entry in the country.

The National bank of Jefferson, Ohio, is found to be $50,000 short.

Wednesday, James Clark, of Pittsburg, shot and killed his wife.

The mercury stood at 39° in Chicago, yesterday, above freezing point.

Herr Most, the foreign socialist, has lectured in Chicago. His utterances were temperate.

Addie Ayers, of Kansas City, is charged with shooting and killing Jacob Blibe, a musician.

Jesse Spaulding is named in Chicago as the successor of David Davis in the United States senate.

Some of the responsible officials of Louisville, Ky., are under a cloud for alleged frauds on the city.

The pig iron manufacturers of Pittsburg are holding a meeting to form a tariff protective association.

Charley Branch, a negro at Akadelphia, Ark., ravished and killed a colored girl, Tuesday. He was arrested.

Levi T. Kretzschmer, for two years secretary of the Arkansas state senate, committed suicide at Vernon, Tuesday.

J. B. Lindsley was shot dead Monday at James bayou, Missouri. His murderer is in the hands of a mob and lynching is expected.

General Sherman denounces as intentionally false the statement in the Sun that he had been received into the Roman Catholic church.

The sale of reserved seats for the Langtry engagement at Haverly's began in Chicago, yesterday. About 200 people were in line all day.

At Syracuse, N. Y., Wednesday, Annie O'Brien, while drawing water, fell into the cistern. Her mother tried to save her and both were drowned.

Judge Winoux, of New York, Wednesday decided the suit of Williams against the Western Union to prevent the payment of dividends on $35,000,000 capital.

The co-operative dress association, in New York, started a year ago with Kate Field as president, has closed its stores. Liabilities $125,000, with al 1 ged assets of $244,000.
j-b-lindsey-james-bayou-1882-12-25.A11:
Christmas Crimes.
Christmas, though passed in a quiet manner all over the country, was a dark day in the criminal record. The telegraph notes the following: Two Frenchmen, names unknown, quarreled at Idaho Springs, this state, when one was shot in the cheek. At Huntsville, Alabama, Carl Southgraw, a despondent tailor, suicided by the revolver route. At Lafayette, Indiana, a drunken man shot and severely wounded two little girls who were walking along a street. At Little Rock, Arkansas, H. T. Robinson, in a dispute with Griffin Robinson (colored), shot the latter dead. In a row among some New York Italians, one of them mortally wounded two of his comrades. In a Christmas fight at Atlanta, Georgia, Henry Johnson killed Hugh Mathes, and at Palmetta, same state, John Thomas killed Lindsey Weaver, in a drunken row. An incendiary burned the farm of Mrs. Mary Winston, in which four horses and fifteen cows perished, and a large amount of property was destroyed. Near Berryville, Arkansas, Rachel Good (colored) gave birth to an illegitimate child, and she and her mother were detected in the act of strangling it. At South Charleston, Kentucky, John Franklin, a colored prisoner, placed in jail for disorderly conduct, assaulted the marshal, Joseph N. Way, and was shot dead in his cell. A band of rioters attempted to take possession of Petersburg, Virginia, terrorizing the town. Charles Row, tired of life, and disgraced by the arrest of his father for horse stealing, suicided at Lafayette, Indiana. At Greencastle, Indiana, Mrs. Myra J. Osborn and her seventeen-year-old son were found dead in their bed; the supposition is that the mother poisoned her son, and then suicided. Timothy Breen and Pat Mooney, two Leadville miners, quarreled in a Harrison avenue saloon, when Breen shot and mortally wounded Mooney, and fled to the mountains, with asheriff and posse in hot pursuit. He subsequently surrendered, had a preliminary examination, and is out on $10,000 bail. BELTON, May 23.—About 1 o'clock, Saturday night, a mob of masked men went to the jail and called for F. King, the jailor, and being informed by Mrs. King that he was absent, they demanded of her the keys to the jail door, and which she was compelled to surrender. Then about twenty-five of the number went to jail and broke into the cells, and let out James Keys colored, and Sam. Shelton white, carried them about a half mile from the jail and hung them to a live oak standing in the forks of the public road where they were found yesterday morning and brought to the court-house where they remained all day Sunday. Jim Keys was put in jail charged with aggravated assault, and Sam Shelton was charged with assault and battery with intent to kill Deputy Sheriff Cresswell about a week ago. Sam Shelton has been charged with several different crimes in this county, but always managed to beat the law, and was never convicted. Jim Keys was a notorious negro, and his many troubles made him put in the greater portion of his time working on the streets or paying fines. There is no clue as to who composed the mob nor upon what ground they were hung, but it seems to be the supposition of some that they were hung for some crime unknown to the public. Wires were down last night, preventing an earlier report.

FROM CARIZZO PASS. Alarming Presence of Apaches —Driven to Texas by Mexican Gauchos. Special Telegram to the Examiner. CARIZZO PASS, TEXAS, May 23.—This mining, prospecting and hunting camp, one hundred and thirteen miles east of El Paso, is much excited by the close proximity of large parties of hostile Apaches passing north-west at distances of from three to fifteen miles from here and are often in full sight. Last night their camp fires were visible on three-sep rate peak. The hostiles are making their way back from Mexico to north-west Texas and New Mexico, having been driven from the south of the Rio Grande by Mexicans who are making Indian killing one of the chief industries in the northern part of the republic to secure the bounty of $300 offered by the Mexican government for every scalp taken of hostile Indians Col. Baylor, of the Texas state ranger, and fifteen of his men have arrived here from the west since Sunday, and depart-
ed this morning, with ten days rations, on a scouting pursuit after the hostiles through the Gaudalupe mountains. Carizzo Pass is the only point where the retreating hostiles can get through the Gaudalupe mountains on their way from Old Mexico to north west Texas and New Mexico, and mining parties and prospectors generally fear an attack, but are keeping close together and are prepared for emergencies. The presence of Major Baylor's men may divert the hostiles from the old trail through the pass to points further west or east. No murders have yet been reported but news of some is hourly feared.

FROM BELTON.

Lynch Law of the Same Old Kind.

BELTON, May 22.—Last Saturday night between 1 and 2 o'clock, an organized mob of about 100 masked men visited the Belton jail and took from its cells two of the inmates—Sam Shelton, white, and Jim Keys, colored—and carried them out about three-quarters of a mile from the public square and hung them to a live-oak tree until they were dead. The tree on which they were hung stands in the public road. They were hanging immediately over the road, consequently they were found early yesterday without much searching. The jury of inquest has not given a verdict as yet, but they will doubtless give in a verdict that they came to their death from being hanged from a tree. Shelton has been charged with several different crimes in this county, but has never been convicted of any of them. He was put in jail about a week ago for assaulting with intent to kill Deputy Sheriff Craswell. His youngest brother, Carroll Shelton, was also put in jail at the same time, being charged with the same offense. Jim Keys was put in jail, being charged with aggravated assault, but he was a very mean, impudent negro, and has been employed working out the fines upon the street and lying in the calaboose the most of his time for the last two years.

BELTON--THE OLD, OLD STORY.
BELTON--THE OLD, OLD STORY.

The Belton special to the Galveston News, republished on our first page, is strange, very strange reading. The Examiner heard, day before yesterday, that Judge Lynch had been holding court at Belton, and earnest efforts were made by this paper Monday to obtain telegraphic particulars for the Examiner of yesterday morning. We wired more than one prominent gentleman in Belton for details, but not a word came in reply, so the paper went to press silent as to the tragedy, rather than publish mere rumors. We said this dispatch is strange reading, and it is. Eight years ago when a similar ghastly scene, (but involving the murder of a far larger number of unfortunate prisoners) was enacted at Belton it was bad enough. But now it seems all but incredible that such a thing should occur. Belton is a large town now and the machinery of legal and social order is far superior to what it was eight years ago. Of course it would be manifestly unjust to hold Belton or Bell county, as a community responsible for such happenings. There is as large a proportion of good people there as anywhere in the state, and their cheeks must tinge with shame as they think of this lynching. It is very plain though that Bell county is cursed with a lawless element that would not be tolerated in any other county in the state as populous, as generally civilized as Bell. One can only feel sorrow for the good people who must loathe this devilish mob domination, and are yet powerless to shake off its rule.

THE BELTON MURDERERS
Pen Pictures of the Two Victims.
Judge Lynch's recent special term of court in our sister city of Belton was a general topic of conversation yesterday, and it is hardly necessary to say the occurrence was quite generally deplored, for Belton and Bell county have strong ties on the friendship of Waco. The surprise was almost as marked as the regret, it having been supposed that with the advent of railways, telegraphs, etc., the old mob element in Bell county would become pow-rless and seek new fields and pastures green, further toward the setting sun. This latest tragedy very naturally recalled similar occurrences in the afflicted county during the past few years—such as the murder of the nine prisoners in jail in 1874; the ducking of Preacher Honey; the whipping of Dr. Russell; the strapping of the Dow brothers, etc. Said one gentleman: "I thought Belton had had her last mob. I am sorry for this, for there are good people out there and they are over-nawed by the mob element." An EXAMINER representative asked a gentleman who, until very recently has resided in Belton, if he knew the victims of Saturday night's work? "Yes," was the reply, "knew them both very well, and I cannot imagine why in the world they were lynched. Sam Shelton, the white man, was probably the most harmless man in the village. He was simply a drunken loafer, as you may see in every town, who had got in bad odor. Often accused of and tried for crookedness and meanness, he was yet never convicted, and I know that he didn't have money to give lawyers big fees, neither was his social standing of the sort to influence a jury in his favor. He was simply no account, and his chief sin seems to have been that he made an attack on a deputy sheriff out there. Jim Key, the negro, was on the same order as Shelton, loafing, hang around saloons, arrested and pay fines or work it out on the streets. He was a saucy negro, if a man would allow him to be, but teach him his place and Jim worked all right. That these two miserable wretches, guilty of no specific and e trainly no proved crime, should be selected for mob practice, is what surprises me. Had they been atrocious murderers, rapists or horse thieves it would not be astonishing. I suppose, though, the mob were getting rusty and wanted to keep their hand in, as the saying is." The reporter asked: "Could the Belton jail be stormed easily by a mob?" The reply was: "Two or three determined, well-armed men could hold it against a mob of a hundred."

A Negro Attacked in His Cabin and Killed—Several Parties Wounded.
KNOXVILLE, Dec. 27.—The Tribune has information of a terrible tragedy, which occurred in the mountainous part of Hawkins county, about sixty miles north of here, last Saturday night. Some white men went to the house of a negro named Gray for the purpose of whipping him, charging that he had stolen hogs. Admittance was denied, whereupon they fired into Gray's cabin. Gallatin News, 4.

Our special correspondent from Big Timber sends us the following:

BIG TIMBER, July 6, 1862.

News has just arrived here that Miss Flora Cutler, school teacher at Sweet Grass, was early this morning shot and supposed to be mortally wounded by Joe Harrison. It is understood here that it is a love affair. Harrison fired four shots at his victim, two of which took effect, one through the right lung, the other in the left arm.

LATER.

6 p.m.—Harrison was arrested immediately after the shooting occurred by private citizens and brought to the justice's court at Big Timber, but too late for examination. Trial was set for to-morrow morning at nine o'clock. The prisoner was put under a guard of private citizens, no sheriff or constable being in the vicinity.

During the morning about three o'clock of the 7th, the guard, consisting of W. H. Brown, Walter Ewing and Ben Howeseth, were overpowered by a mob of twenty to thirty unmasked men, who took the prisoner and hung him to the building where he was guarded. The mob then left, crossing the river at Kiger's ferry, forcing the ferryman to put them over. A coroner's jury will be empaneled at Big Timber before R. B. Dunham, J. GOSSIP ABOUT THE SHOOTING.

There is much loose gossip in Bozeman about the murder and what inspired or led to it. Last night a gentleman told us, at the LaClede, that Miss Cutler and Mr. Harrison, eight years since attended as pupils, the same school in Minnesota, since which time they have been correspond-ing,—it being generally understood that there was an engagement.

On July Fourth Mr. Harrison and Miss Cutler attended a ball at the Countryman House, Stillwater, and while there several scenes took place which were sadly out of joint.

At one time during the progress of the dancing, Miss Cutler was seen by her escort dancing with another gentleman. This sight set amidst the beauty, gayety and music of that evening, which inspires us all, so maddened Mr. Harrison that he rushed out of the room and made a break for the Yellowstone, saying: "I will drown myself." It took the strenuous exertions of several men to prevent him from accomplishing his threat. After returning to Sweet Grass on the night of July 4th it seemed that green-eyed jealousy consumed him until the morning of the 6th, when Miss Cutler was shot.

ATEMPT TO COMMIT AN OUTRAGE.
The Perpetrator Summarily Dealt with.
Week before last, a negro named John
The Perpetrator Summarily Dealt with.

Week before last a negro named John Mullins, attempted to commit a nameless outrage upon Mrs. Smith, wife of Thos. Smith, who lives in the south-western part of Lawrence, near the Lincoln county line. Being near home at the time, Mrs. Smith soon reached there and informed her husband, who mounted his horse and went in pursuit. He overtook him, and fired upon him, hitting him in the leg. The negro ran, and Mr. Smith fired again, hitting him in some portion of the body, but Mullins succeeded in eluding capture. It was afterwards learned that he had concealed himself in a sink-hole, and Mr. Smith had passed near him several times. After everything became quiet he dragged himself to a negro house near by, and from there he was carried to his sister's, who lives on Topisaw, near Tyler's mill, in this county. On last Thursday night, 10th inst., a crowd of men, supposed to be about fifteen, went to the place and called for Mike Mullins, his brother, but were told he was not there. They then called for Jno. Mullins, and the answer came that he was unable to get up. The men outside ordered him to sit up on the bed. This he did. Two boards were pulled from the side of the house, guns placed in the opening and two shots fired into Mullins. The crowd outside then ordered those in the house to cover up their heads and keep them covered under penalty of death. Three of the men entered the house and fired twice more into the body of Mullins, though it is thought he was killed by the shots fired from the outside. They walked to the bed, crossed Mullin's hands, closed his eyes and then rode away.

Editorial Items.
Congress was in session eight months.

Judge M. Levy, one of the Supreme court Judges of Louisiana, died last week.

Mr. Menilaus, of Lincoln county, in this State, has raised fifteen acres of jute.

Harrison county has money loaned on interest.

The Indians are committing depredations in Arizona territory.

It takes $10 in paper money to buy $1 in gold in Buenos Ayres, S. A.

W. F. Blackman has been elected Judge of the 12th Judicial district of Louisiana.

Gen. Grant has been appointed a commissioner to negotiate a commercial treaty with Mexico.

The question whether it is right to keep a savage bulldog in a churchyard to bite ma- rauders, is puzzling a Milwaukee vestry.

The case of the Detroit negro convicted of marrying a white girl is to be made a test of the Fifteenth Amendment.

The Boonville Pleader announces that Mrs. Fallis, wife of Mr. N. L. Fallis, was struck and instantly killed by lightning during the storm Tuesday afternoon.

John Mullins, a negro, attempted to commit an outrage on a white lady in Lawrence county, recently. A crowd of men captured Mullins and shot him to death.

Maj. Andrew S Herron, of Baton Rouge, has been nominated for Congress by the Democrats of the Sixth District of Louisiana, in place of E. W. Robertson.

Georgia's great Senator, Benjamin H. Hill, after long suffering, died in Atlanta, Ga., on the morning of the 16th. His last words were, "Almost Home."

There is a farmer in Ohio who has not sheared his sheep in five years, because, as he claims, Providence intended for the sheep to wear their wool.

One morning last week the mail was robbed between Shreveport and Minden by two masked men. Thirteen registered letters were secured by the robbers. Four passengers and the driver were relieved of their money and valuables.

The Nebraska young man who broke the leg of a rival in a combat over a girl whom both were encouraged to love does not feel that he was the victor after all, since she has taken to devotedly nursing the invalid, and has promised to marry him as soon as he can walk to church.

Even the Indians are becoming prohibitionists out West. Some of the red men at the Pine Ridge agency, Dakota, have asked the agent to post notices offering $50 reward for evidence by which any person is convicted of furnishing liquor to Indians under the law, and the savages will themselves pay the money.

A. B Camp, a miner at San Benite, Cal., left his family in New England, years ago, and went West to seek his fortune. Having prospered, he sent for his wife. He was in the mine when she arrived, and there she followed him, getting an affectionate reception. They started to leave the mine, he going in advance, when a part of the tunnel caved in, and she was killed.

The Chicago Railway Age reports 969 miles of new railway laid in the United States during July, making the total construction for the seven months of the year that have passed, 5,959 miles. Last year at this time barely 3,000 miles was reported. The total railway mileage of the country is now 110,770 miles, and it assumes that the total construction of new road this year will be 10,000 miles, against 9 358 miles last year.

john-wagner-ironton-1882-01-19.A2:
JACKSON, OHIO, THURSDAY, DECEMBER 22, 1881.
Another Murder Near Ironton.
The good people of Ironton have been considerably excited on account of a murder just east of the city limits. Dr. Joseph A. Beggs was clerk at Etna Iron Works, and an eminent chemist. He was shot and killed near eleven o'clock at night, by Bill Zeck and John Wagoner. We have carefully read the testimony taken at the Coroner's inquest, as reported in the Ironton papers, and there appears to be considerable mystery about it. The case appears to be mixed up with bad women, beer and tobacco. The murderers, and the persons who were present, testify that a man came to Wagoner's house and commenced whistling and kicking against the fence. He was asked what he wanted, and what his name was. He said his name was "Old Hell." When he would not go away they shot him. There is other evidence, tending to show that the murder was committed at a point on the railroad, and not at Wagoner's house.

The citizens of Ironton have held a meeting, and passed resolutions requesting Judge Harper to hold a special term of Court to try the murderers. They also appointed a committee to raise money for the widow and children of the murdered man.

The Ironton papers speak of Dr. Beggs as a quiet, inoffensive, moral, good citizen. People sometimes differ on these questions. In Ironton, it seems, a man may spend his time and money at a beer hell until near midnight, smoking cigars and swilling beer, and yet be a model of morality in that moral city. Fanatics, like ourself, view it in a different light. In order to explain our meaning, we publish part of the testimony of two or three of the witnesses:

Jesse W. Maynard.—Myself. Cyrus Palmer and Lafayette Mead were going home from Ironton about 10 and 11 o'clock and stopped at Lion Garden to get a drink just before and the saloon keeper were sitting there reading and smoking. We went out again, and Palmer and I stood and talked 15 or 20 minutes, and sitting on Beggs came out of the saloon and walked just in and turned off the path to the right just by the Le Page house. We kept on up the plike, and about the third telegraph post above elm tree house heard some one say, "there goes the dragon and a cigar, and in the air on a keeper heard a gun fire, and in a short time heard another shot; thought a little further down and a fainter pistol.

Henry Fisher, proprietor of Lion Garden, and his son, also testified. Mr. Beggs came into the saloon about 8 or 9. In a short time, Palmer and his partners came in, got a glass of beer each, and went out. Beggs carried a cigar, and took a glass of beer there. When the three men went out, he was the only customer left, and he remained quite a time with Mr. Fisher. He had taken another beer at the bar, and finally took another beer at the bar. He passed out a little before ten, the Fishers thought, and was seen by them for a few steps, going up the road.
john-wagner-ironton-1882-01-19.A4:
LYNCHED IN OHIO.
One Murderer Hanged, and Another Swung Up and Forced to Confess.
CINCINNATI, January 20.—John Waggoner, who murdered Dr. Briggs, Treasurer of the Alice Furnace Company, two months ago, was taken out of jail at Ironton, Ohio, between twelve and one o'clock last night and lynched in the court house yard by from forty to sixty masked men. They first took Bill Seek, the other accused murderer, and swung him up, whereupon he made a confession implicating others not yet arrested, and the crowd allowed him to live for the present. There is not the slightest clue to the perpetrators, and public opinion seems to approve of the lynching.
john-wagner-ironton-1882-01-19.A5:
ONLY TWO HANGINGS.
Anderson Jones Pays the Penalty Under the Forms of Law, But Ohio Lynchers Attend to John Wagner.
John Wagoner Lynched.

IRONTON, O., Jan. 20.—John Wagoner, one of the murderers of Dr. Joseph Biggs, who was shot after night on a lonesome path near the Etna Iron works nearly two months ago, was taken from the county jail by a well-organized band last night, and hanged in the court house yard. One of his accomplices, Wm. Zeck, was also taken out, and with the rope around his neck made a confession that there was an organized band in the vicinity for murder and robbery. Dr. Beggs was killed for his money, but they only got one silver dollar. He said Biggs was either killed by Sarah Zeck, John Wagoner or Frank Marshall. He says he himself was in the house at the time Mrs. Wagoner, mother of John, told them to tie a bar of pig iron to Beggs' neck and sink the body in the river, but then concluded to try a different plan, and carried the body where it was found, and then went after the officers and told them they had killed him in self defense; but the people were morally certain, from the glaring improbabilities embodied in the history, that Beggs had been murdered. The developments of last night have proved that this opinion was correct. After his confession Zeck was returned to the jail. Wagoner refused to say anything, and was strung up to a tree.

When a man is hung by a mob in Ohio they break the news gently. One John Wagoner was lynched at Ironton, Ohio, last Friday night, as mentioned in our dispatches the next day. A special to the Cincinnati Commercial, givse a long account of the affair, from which the following sentences are culled:

Last night for the first time in the history of Lawrence county, the slow process of the law was dispensed with, and speedy, inflexible justice administered to one murderer at least. Your readers are by this time all familiar with the murder of Dr. Joseph Beggs, last November, an event which at the time filled this community with horror. Directly after the murder there were many threats of lynching. So many murders had been committed within the last few years in this country, and so many murderers, through the stupidity and rascality of jurors, gone unhanged, that the community and the best citizens were almost desperate. Things seemed to have reached a most dangerous state, and it was the general opinion that something radical would have to soon be done. This feeling threatened a long rope and a short shrift to the murderers.

Everything so far had been done with the regularity of macinery, and with absolutely no noise, confusion or outery. It was no mob made of the rabble got together in the excitement of the moment, that was doing these things. There were not more than forty or fifty in the band. All were masked. Each had his number. There was not only a leader, but also Captains of squads. All orders were given to the numbers, it was "No. 9 here." The commands were in a low and disguised tone. Everything evinced careful drill by intelligent men.

Lynch law in any but unorganized communities is a most dangerous and destructive thing. We trust, however, that if good results can possibly flow from its exercise, this terrible affair will have its lasting lesson. It may possibly strike terror into the hearts of an element that too little fears justice as administered in our courts.

As soon the guards over them were removed the mob dispersed, no one knows whither. Not a soul, so far as is known, recognized anyone of the band of lynchers. They were effectively disguised.

And all this in the glorious climate of Ohio. The only remark made by the Commercial editorially is this: "The hanging of John Wagoner by an organized body of masked men is but the prelude of what is coming if the law is not more efficiently and sternly administered in this country." This man no doubt, deserved hanging, but the mob had no more right
john-wagner-ironton-1882-01-19.A18:
More Lynch Law.
Our readers will remember that several weeks ago we mentioned the murder of Dr. Beggs, near Ironton. He was shot as he was going home from a saloon, about eleven o'clock at night. A man named Zeek, and another named Waggoner, were arrested and sent to jail. Zeek has made a confession, and says that Waggoner, who is his brother-in-law, did the shooting.

On just Thursday night a mob of disguised men took Waggoner out of the jail and hung him on a tree, near the Court House.

We believe, the way the criminal law is now not being administered, that this was right. In order to make lynch law a terror to evil-doers, it must extend, in some cases, to Judges and jurors.

A short time ago the Ironton Bee had an editorial in favor of abolishing juries, and among other sensible things said:

Our own county is a sad illustration of the evils of the jury system. We are over $13,000 in debt on our expense fund alone, because juries have failed both of defendants who infested the immediate vicinity of Hanging Rock, when at last brought into Court, escaped through the Jury. One languishes in the penitentiary. But not because he committed the bonest acts on the calendar. The Jury absorbed that, because one of the members didn't want to "dissagree the family." But the criminal unwittingly plead guilty to perjury, and the judge (most noble Judge I) gave him the shortest sentence the law allowed.

The county bears the expense of these useless prosecutions. The Jury says in effect to the criminal, "Well done!" and to his associates, "Go thou, and do likewise."

It is no safety for life or property, no protection or satisfaction in law. Ignorant men make the best jurors, and ignorant men are the most bigoted and obstinate. There are many bad features in our laws which need to be remedied, but the worst of them all is the criminal jury.

Between Judge Lynch and the modern jury, with its ineptible sprinkling of "smart alcoaks" and obstinate ignoramuses, we are decidedly of the opinion, the former would be much more speedy and effectual than the latter.
Between Judge Lynch and the modern jury, with its ineptly sprinkling of "smart alceks" and obstinate ignoramuses, we are decidedly of the opinion, the former would be much more speedy and effectual in the suppression of crime. The people will be compelled to take the law, their own hands, and our opinion is to do it, the better, if these outbreaking crimes continue.

Self-protection is the first law of nature, and when it has been fully demonstrated that the law is incapable of protecting them, it is time tozeno project himself and his family. If it becomes necessary to drive out the whole set of soundrels from whom these outrages emanate, let the citizens organize and do it thoroughly. In other words, let us have peace and order, if we have to fight for it.

And to our Legislators let us say: "Away with the Jury!"

Mob Law in Ohio.

John Wagoner, in jail at Ironton, Lawrence County, Ohio, charged with the murder of Dr. Joseph Beggs, of that place, last November, was taken from jail by fifty masked men on the night of January 19 and hanged to a tree in the court-house yard. The crime of which Wagoner was guilty was a very atrocious and unprovoked one, and was committed, it has been thought, for the purpose of robbery. Dr. Beggs was a bookkeeper for an iron company, and was assaulted and murdered while on his way home from the mill, after dark had set in. Wagoner and a man named Zeek, toward whom suspicion so strongly pointed that there was little doubt remained as to their guilt, were arrested charged with the crime. On the night in question, few minutes after 12 o'clock, a knock was heard at the jail, and the Sheriff responded by opening the door. He was seized, overpowered and with cocked revolvers the mob demanded the keys of the jail. The Sheriff firmly refused, and seeing that he would not yield, he was taken into the room of his wife where the demand was repeated in a similar manner. His wife, frightened almost out of her senses, surrendered the keys, and in a moment the door to the cell in which Wagoner and Zeek were confined was swung open and the prisoners were led trembling from the cell. "I didn't mean to kill him," protested Wagoner in a tone of agony, but his words were unheeded and he was hurried into the yard and hanged without any ado. Zeek was so thoroughly frightened that he was scarcely able to stand and was terrorized into a confession. Zeek thought his time had come, and with a countenance ashy pale, related the circumstances of the killing as best he could. His confession was to the effect that he was an accomplice, and that Wagoner did the killing. After Beggs had been struck down, Mrs. Zeek (Zeek's wife) and a Mrs. Hall carried the body of the dead man from the scene to where it was afterward found. After Zeek's confession he was returned to his cell and locked up, evidently the mob desiring to keep him for further testimony respecting those whom he implicated. What Wagoner had to say in his last moments is not known. It is sufficient to know that in two minutes after he was taken from the jail he was suspended by the neck under a tree only a few feet from the court-house. The mob was very orderly in their work, being headed by a leader and all answering promptly to their numbers, showing that they had all been well drilled for the job in advance. Several belated citizens who hap-
their work, being headed by a leader and all answering promptly to their numbers, showing that they had all been well drilled for the job in advance. Several belated citizens who happened to pass while the mob were carrying out their work, were halted by the guards stationed about and kept prisoners until the work was completed. The mob then quietly dispersed, going in all directions. The body of Wagoner was allowed to hang until morning when it was viewed and cut down by the Coroner and handed over to an undertaker. Wagoner was said to be a rather good looking fellow, with mild blue eyes, aquiline nose, mustache and a well shaped face. His features bore no evidence of hanging. Mrs. Hall and Mrs. Zeek were arrested in the morning on the strength of Zeek's confession, but at the time of their arrest they had no knowledge of Wagoner's fate, or Zeek's confession, and asserted their innocence and entire willingness to go with the officers.
john-wagner-ironton-1882-01-19.A21:
JUDGE LYNCH
Settles With John Wagoner.
IRONTON O., Jan. 21.—One night last November Dr. Josep Beggs was found about a mile from this town riddled with buckshot. The morning after his murder John Waggoner and Wm. Zeck were arrested, charged with the crime. A preliminary examination was held before Mayor Corns, and the two were committed without bail to answer the charge of murder in the first degree. Both Waggoner and Zeek were disreputable men, and belonged to disreputable families. The fact that two such degraded rascals had taken the life of so valuable a citizen as Dr. Beggs was enough aside from the terrible features surrounding the crime, to excite the community to a dangerous pitch of rage.

Threats of summary vengeance were heard on every side. The indignation was too intense to be smothered. Shortly after twelve o'clock last night Sheriff Kimball was aroused by a knocking at the jail door and getting up, went to answer it. No sooner did he open the door than, quick as a flash, he was seized by a band of masked men lying in wait outside, who told him that they didn't intend to hurt him, and ordered him to keep quiet. Before he could recover from his amazement three or four cocked revolvers were leveled at his head, and a stern, determined voice demanded of him the keys to the jail. The Sheriff, in his hurry to answer the knocking had come to the door in his undercloths, and of course did not have the keys with him. He was ordered to tell where they were. Being a men of grit he refused to do this. The talk so far had taken place in the hall, and then the masked gang some ten or fifteen in number marched him to the room that he had left, and renewed the demand. Again, a flat refusal. It looked as if the mob would be forced to beat down the doors or be baffled. But in this room was the Sheriff's wife. She, terrified by the midnight attack, the threats and the deadly looking revolvers, told the lynchers where the keys were. They unlocked the cell door, took Waggoner out into the Court House yard and hung him to the limb of a tree.
john-wagner-ironton-1882-01-19.A27: JOHN WAGNER was hanged by a mob, in the Ironton, (Ohio) court yard on the 19th inst., for the murder of Dr. BEGGS. The encouragement given to mob law by the Athens Messenger, St. Clairsville Gozette and other papers in Ohio, is calculated to foster a spirit of outlawry that is fearful to contemplate. The laws are ample for the punishment of the perpetrators of crimes, however revolting and terrible they may be, and the countenancing of any other mode of procedure is to be deprecated in the strongest language possible. In Athens County the lynchers of Davis have not been arrested, and the Coroner's inquest returned a verdict—Came to his death at the hands of persons unknown to the jury. It is alleged that a number of the lynchers are and were known at the time of the inquest to the entire population of Albany and Athens. Comment is unnecessary, especially so, when we reflect for a moment upon the boasted civilization of our modern Athens.

DAILY EVENING BULLETIN. TUESDAY EVENING, JAN. 31, 1882.
AGAIN the wedding bells ring out,
Their joyous tones reminding,
Kindred souls, the God of Love
In wedded bliss are binding
God keep the sunshine in their hearts,
Their plighted faith unbroken,

john-wagner-ironton-1882-01-19.A30: On the night of January 19th, John Wagner, who had murdered Dr. Beggs, was taken from the jail at Ironton, Ohio, by citizens and hanged. The circumstances of the murder were peculiarly atrocious, and there was no question of the prisoner's guilt. The summary act was prompted by the acquittal on a legal technicality of a murderer in an adjoining county. The people had cause to fear that justice would not be done by the courts, and for this good reason took the matter into their own hands.

A Fighting Negro.
TARBORO (N. C.), Oct. 23.—Constable Durford of this place arrested Louis Guilford, a negro, for an assault. On the way to jail Guilford drew a razor and cut Durford across the abdomen, inflicting a terrible wound. As Durford sank to the ground to die Guilford ran off. He was pursued and captured, but seriously wounded two of his captors. He was finally shot and mortally wounded.

A ROBBER TORN BY DOGS. While David J. McKinney, a junk dealer, of Lebanon county, Pa., was on his way home from Fredericksburg, and when in the vicinity of Red Bridge, a man came out of the woods and stopped his team and demanded his money. McKinney told the highway robber that he had no money, whereupon he ordered him from the wagon, at the same time drawing a revolver. Mr. McKinney had three mastiff dogs with him, and immediately called them and put them on the robber. A terrible struggle ensued. One of the dogs attacked him in front, while the other two jumped at him from behind. Every stitch of clothing was torn from the robber's body. The dogs were very ferocious, and would no doubt have torn the man te pieces had Mr. McKinney not called them away. A party shortly after made search, but could find nothing of the wherabouts of the robber, but it is thought he is badly hurt.

STUPENDOUS TAXATION.—No country in the history of the world has ever paid such taxes as the United States under republican rule. All the paper in circulation amounts only to 600,000,000. In the seventeen years since the war the Government has collected from the people $6,000,-000, that is, if paper money only had been used, every dollar of it would have passed into the Treasury ten times! The government receipts last year were nearly twice as much as the value of the entire cotton crop. The government receipts were nearly $400,000,000. The cotton crop amounted to 5,400,000 bales, selling for $50 a bale. Such taxation, says the Raleigh News and Observer, is monstrous and is the reason that the people are not prosperous. The success of the democratic party will change all this, and the people will be freed from the oppression that now burthens them.

THE TELEGRAPH EXPLAINED.—A couple of colored gents were standing about the Relay depot yesterday, awaiting the departure of their train. They observed nearly everything about the locality, and commented upon the same. The numerous telegraph wires about the depot did not escape their notice, and one of them expressed his wonder at the rapidity with which a message could be sent a great distance.

"Why, that's easy enough to understand," said the other.

"How?"

"Well, suppose you had a dog 3,000 miles long—"

"Pshaw! You can't have a dog 3,000 miles long."

"I know that; but we suppose that there was one. Don't you understand me?"

"Well, what then?"

"You take this dog, 3,000 miles long, and place his fore feet in New York and his hind feet in California—"

"What then?"

"You just tramp on this dog's tail in California and you bet he'll growl in New York."

"That's so," said the darkey, and he assumed an expression of deep thought while the other appeared quite satisfied with his apt and original illustration of the telegraph.

KNIFE AND PISTOL.
A BATCH OF HOME CHRISTMAS
TRAGEDIES.
A Bloody Affair at Waycross—A Woman Deliberately Shot—Horrible Stabbing Affray—A Deadly Quarrel at Dupont—Riot at Oconee—Fears of Further Trouble.

WAYCROSS, GA., Dec. 25.—Joe Styles and W. H. Otten, colored, while under the influence of liquor here to-day, got into a quarrel, during which Styles cut Otten's throat, inflicting a mortal wound. Styles escaped.

To-night William Davis, colored, met Mollie Baker, colored, on the railroad, deliberately pulled out his pistol and shot her, inflicting a serious wound in the thigh. No words passed between them. Davis was arrested.

Saturday night, at Dupont, Ga., a negro named Dennis Claybon was cut by Jud Mathas, white. A crowd of negroes were standing on the railroad track, some dancing and playing the banjo. Some insulting words passed between Mathas and Claybon. Mathas went off, bought a knife and returned and attacked Claybon, cutting him on the right cheek, severing his ear and exposing the right jaw from ear to mouth. The wound is not considered fatal.

SANDERSVILLE, GA., Dec. 26.—A riot occurred at Oconee yesterday between several negroes and white citizens, which resulted in the shooting of three negroes, one of whom will probably die, and Mr. Webster, the Town Marshal, who was seriously injured, but from last accounts was doing very well. On Saturday last several negroes under the influence of liquor became very troublesome, and the Marshal arrested one. On Monday they returned armed, as it seems, to have a difficulty, which was very unexpected by the citizens. The whites sent word to Toomsboro this afternoon for help, as they were expecting trouble from the negroes to-night.

THE OCONEE RIOT.
The Town Marshal's Son Shot and a Negro Mortally Wounded. TOONSBORO GA. Dec. 15. The
The Town Marshal's Son Shot and a Negro Mortally Wounded.

TOOMSBORO, GA., Dec. 15.→The Marshal at Oconee, upon attempting to arrest some negroes who were fighting, was resisted, and a general fight ensued, in which Mayor Snell and sons and the Marshal and his son participated. The negroes fired the first pistol, shooting the Marshal's son, who, after he was hit, put two bullets into a negro. One negro was mortally wounded.

This occurred on Monday. On Tuesday the whites heard rumors of a rescue by the negroes of the prisoners, and they sent here for aid. The Marshal with a posse of ten was sent down. All is quiet now, and it is hoped that matters will remain so.
marshal-fight-oconee-1882-12-11.A5:
A Marshal Attacked by Negroes.
MACON, Ga., Dec. 30.—A row between a family of drunken negroes and the Marshal of Oconee on Christmas Day led to the report of a riot there. The Washington brothers (colored), five in number, resisted arrest, attacking the Marshal. The citizens went to his assistance, while a negro desperado named Ira Lawson assisted the Washington brothers. Knives and pistols were drawn by both parties, and three whites and four negroes were wounded. Ira Lawson was the only person seriously hurt.

MARSHAL DAVID SNODGRASS, of Crestline, was shot and killed on the 21st. A man with no visible means of support had been hanging about town for several days, and the Marshal was watching him. While in a hardware store taking to Dr. Jenner, the man entered and asked to be shown some cartridges. The Marshal stepped up to the fellow and, after asking several questions about himself, asked him if he had a revolver. He replied that he had one at home. The Marshal then took hold of him, but the fellow tore away and ran, the Marshal and Dr. Jenner in hot pursuit. Before going four rods he turned and fired at the Marshal. Dr. Jenner then started in pursuit, hallooing "Catch that thief!" The pursued man then fired again, which struck the Marshal near the heart. Dr. Jenner, who was close behind the Marshal, saw the second shot had taken effect, and took Snodgrass into a drug-store, where he died in about seven minutes. The murderer was pursued by others, who by this time had joined in the chase, and finally captured and it was with great difficulty that the infuriated citizens were kept from lynching the fellow. Several persons however did take the trouble to hit the fellow over the head and beat and bruised him up considerable before he was gotten into the lockup.

Home and Foreign News.
A rother overdow of the Mississippi river is feared.

The Dominion House of Commons, Friday, passed resolutions asking Her Majesty to give Ireland the same form of government enjoyed by Canada.

The Bible on which oaths have been administered in the U. S. Senate during the past fifty-three years, has been stolen. The veteran keeper, Mr. Bassett, who had charge of it, is greatly distressed.

Marshal David Snodgrass, of Centreville, Ono, was shot and killed Friday night by a burglar whom he was trying to arrest. The murderer was taken to jail, but at once taken out by a mob, and probably lynched.

Pacific coast men threaten to boycott Eastern merchants who signed petitions against the Chinese bill.

The extravagance that accompanies a life of crime is illustrated by the fact that, although the robberies in which the late Jesse James participated are said to have exceeded a quarter of a million of dollars, only about $200 are left to his widow.

Rev. Ralph Fothergill, of the Primitive Methodist church, in Fall River, died Friday night of small pox. Four of his children are sick with the disease. He was opposed to vaccination, and would not allow himself or family to be vaccinated.

The New York Tribune prints a sworn statement by Rudolph Razin, formerly a Mormon, that George Q. Cannon in 1855, urged him to murder Alvin W. Babbitt, territorial secretary. Next Alvin W. Babbitt, territorial secretary. Next year Babbitt was killed, as Razin believes at Cannon's institution.

The President has transmitted to Congress the address of the Minister of Mexico to the Secretary of State, proposing conclusion of a convention between the two countries for defining the boundary between the United States and Mexico from the Rio Grande westward to the Pacific Ocean by the erection of the erection to the Pacific Ocean by the President commends the proposal.

It is reported the Chilian authorities have issued an order forbidding the United States men-of-war to receive their mailbags from the Panama steamers as heretofore, and informing the American naval officers on the station that the American mailbags will afterward be delivered by the pursers of the British mail steamers from Panama to the Chilian authorities.

bags will hereafter be delivered by the purchasers of the British mail steamers from Panama to the Chilian authorities.

—Mrs. Tabor, wife of H. A. W. Tabor, Lieutenant-Governor of Colorado, has brought suit for a separate maintenance. Mr. Tabor, although represented as uneducated and rather uncouth, is reported to be the richest man in Colorado, and he nearly succeeded in being elected United States Senator in place of Mr. Teller, now Secretary of the Interior. Mrs. Tabor asks that she be awarded the fine house on Broadway, Denver, which she now lives in, and that it be set apart for her exclusive use. It is the finest residence in Colorado, and is valued at $150,000. She further asks for $50,000 per year for her maintenance, alleging that her husband is worth between $7,000,000 and $8,000,000. The sensational point of the suit lies in the allegation of infidelity.
marshal-snodgrass-crestline-1882-04-21.A13: Marshal Snodgrass, of Crestline, was shot and killed by a tramp, last Friday evening. The Marshal was chasing him to arrest when he turned and fired three times, the second shot passing through the heart. He was assisted into a drug store close by, and almost immediately expired. He leaves a family. The tramp was arrested, and with difficulty saved from violence. He was taken to Bucyrus that evening and lodged in jail.

CONDENSED NEWS.
In his daily walks about Boston, Charles Francis Adams is regularly accompanied by a private detective.

Brooklyn people seem to fear that the Standard Oil company will soon obtain control of the gas business of that city.

The steamer Corwin has sailed for the Arctic regions to relieve the crew of the Rodgers.

James W. Borden, a prominent democrat of Indiana, judge of the criminal court at Fort Wayne, died Tuesday.

Tabor and others have sold the Henriette mine at Leadville to a party of French and English capitalists for $1,-500,000.

In the Dominion house of commons, Mr. Blake's resolution that Canada should negotiate commercial treaties was defeated by a vote of 104 to 58.

The corporation of Marseilles has brought suit against ex-Empress Eugenie to obtain title to the chateau presented under the Napoleonic regime.

Bradlaugh has brought suit against the assistant sergeant-at-arms for ejecting him from the lobby of the British house of commons.

In the United States court at Grand Rapids, Mich., Rev. Mr. Koehler was fined $300 for sending indecent letters to his wife after they had separated.

The sixty-third anniversary of the institution of the order of Odd-Fellows was very generally celebrated Wednesday throughout the United States.

Pinkeye has appeared among the horses in New York, and one sales stable reports the loss of two or three head per day for the past fortnight.

A London journal predicts that before the week closes all the American suspects imprisoned in Ireland will have left the country.

David Snodgrass, marshal of Crestline, O., was shot dead by a stranger, whom he was endeavoring to arrest. The citizens made two attempts to lynch the murderer.

In the suit brought at Washington by Hallett Kilbourne against Sergeant-at-Arms Thompson, for damages for false imprisonment, the jury rendered a verdict for $100,000. A motion for a new trial will be filed.

Henry S. Debevoise, mayor of Long Island City, has been arrested to answer for a deficit of $112,936 in the bond accounts. He refuses to make any statement.

Lemuel L. Crocker, the largest livestock dealer in Buffalo, made an assignment to cover liabilities of nearly $1,-000,000, thereby causing the suspension of Frank A. Sears, a dealer in malt.

Several cigar-makers from Germany, with their families, arrived at Milwaukee Saturday to take the place of strikers, and were escorted to the factories by the police.

The army of India will hereafter consist of 31 regiments of cavalry and 113 of infantry. Four regiments of native cavalry and 19 of infantry are to be disbanded.

Ex-Secretary Kirkwood will not consent to become a candidate for congress in the Fifth district of Iowa. The contest lies between Judge Struble, Senator Arnold, and ex-Senator Rumple.

The fastest regular train ever run between New York and Boston will be placed on the Springfield route May 1. The time will be six hours, and there will be eight stops.

In the city of Kamenetz, Russia, having a population of 22,000, the shops and houses of all Jews were destroyed by incendiary fires, the loss being 500,000 rubles.

A London journal says that Mr. and Mrs. J. W. Mackey have been so pestered by suitors for the hand of their daughter that they have announced that she will receive no marriage portion.

Nearly six thousand persons are thrown out of employment by the closing of the Harmony mills at Cohoes, N. Y. The spinners and weavers saw no reason for a reduction of 10 per pent. in their wages.

The governor of Tennessee has received a proposition from the holders of state bonds to compromise the debt at 60 per cent., with graded interest of 4, 5, and 6 per cent.

Mrs. Saltzeman, of St. Joseph, Mo., who owns the house in which Jesse James was killed, has filed with Governor Crittenden a claim for $2,000 damages, caused by relic-hunters. She holds the state responsible.

The immigration commissioners at New York are at Albany, urging the passage of the bill appropriating $250,-000 for necessary expenses at Castle Garden, in default of which amount the institution will be closed.

In the Guiteau case, the supreme court of the District of Columbia gave Charles H. Reed two weeks to prepare his argument in the bill of exceptions, which will come up May 8. Only that portion of Scoville's letter announcing his withdrawal from the case was read.

LYNCH LAW IN VERMONT.
A MOB OF WEALTHY FARMERS LED BY A JUSTICE OF THE PEACE.
Hanging a Man Accused of Assault, and Giving Him a Coat of Tar and Feathers- Little Evidence of the Victim's Guilt.
Hanging a Man Accused of Assault, and Giving Him a Coat of Tar and Feathers—Little Evidence of the Victim's Guild.

RUTLAND, Vt., July 8.—On Thursday night at about 10 o'clock from fifteen to twenty men surrounded the house of Timothy Coakley, a well-to-do Irish farmer in the town of Shrewsbury, a mountain town a dozen miles east of Rutland. The leaders of the party called at the door and explained that they wanted Paul Ellis, whose reputation was not the best, and whom they charged with attempted criminal assault on the fourteen-year-old daughter of Charles Gleason. Ellis expected to begin working for Mr. Coakley the next day, and had just arrived there. In opposition to the wish of Coakley, but on the assurance of one of the leaders, who is a Justice of the Peace, a number of men crowded into the house and tied a rope around Ellis's waist. The entire mob grasped the rope, which was over thirty feet long, and dragged the man out of the house and down the road to a spot over half a mile from the house. Here a halt was ordered, and the victim was told to prepare for death. The rope was shifted from the man's waist to his neck, and the other end thrown over the limb of a tree. Whether Ellis was actually hanged, or whether he was so frightened that he thought he was, is hard to determine at present. He says that he was pulled up a number of times and threatened with death unless he acknowledged the attempted assault. The lynchers, who talk freely of their exploit, and seem proud of it, said they only threatened. At any rate, Ellis acknowledged nothing, made what he thought was his dying prayers, and admitted a number of petty thefts, all the while begging most piteously for his life. At length he was treated to a coat of tar and feathers, and, more dead than alive, turned loose in the woods. Among the party of lynchers, besides the Justice of the Peace, were a number of influential and wealthy farmers—in fact, every farmer of wealth within a radius of many miles being among them, and the father of the girl, Charles Gleason.

Investigation, in which every prominent actor was interviewed, including the victim of the lynchers, makes the attempted assault somewhat questionable. Gleason, the father of the girl, is a very poor farmer, owning a mountain farm mortgaged for more than it is worth, on which a precarious living only can be made. A tumble-down rookery of a house shelters the father, two girls, and two boys. The mother is rallying from a recent confinement at her brother's, in Boston, for they are too poor at home to furnish proper food and treatment. Forty rods from the house is the district school, with twenty or more pupils, and windows and doors wide open. The alleged attempt occurred on June 19. That morning Ellis was at Gleason's house when the latter left for Rutland. Gleason owes Ellis money, and Ellis says he tried to borrow more, but was refused. Gleason admits that he was trying to get money to pay his taxes with, but denies asking Ellis for it. On the other hand, he charges Ellis with having stolen $5 while he was in the house. After Gleason left the girl commenced churning, and she says that it was while she was at this work that Ellis attempted to assault her, but that she ran into the house. Ellis says that she asked him to help her churn.

Three times Gleason visited the house where Ellis boarded, once meeting him, and each time threatening his life and displaying a large knife. On Thursday Gleason came to Rutland and purchased tar. The lynching was talked of on Wednesday night, but a sufficient crowd could not be got together, and it was put off until Thursday night. In the whole town of Shrewsbury only two families were met with who sided with Ellis—the Coakleys, where the abduction took place, and one other.

Ellis occasionally gets drunk, but is a first-class man on the farm. He gets high wages, hoards a little, and always has money about him. To-day he turned up in Rutland, and, although somewhat sore from being hauled a half mile over a rough road, is in seemingly good condition. The Justice also was in town, and the two met. High words followed, and Ellis was arrested, charged with drunkenness. His trial occurs on Monday morning, in which some of the facts may be brought out.

The people of Rutland, as well as Shrewsbury, uphold the lynchers. This is on account of the poor character of Ellis and the wealth of those engaged in the lynching. Ellis has two brothers here, who have the respect of the community. The local daily newspaper, after giving some meagre facts in relation to the case this morning, came out with a stinging editorial article demanding the punishment of those engaged in the outrage.

Lynch Law in Vermont.
On Thursday evening last a mob at Shrewsbury applied a modified form of lynch law to one Paul Ellis, who had attempted rape. It seems that a week ago Ellis called at the house of one of the most respected families of the town, and finding no one at home but a girl fourteen years of age, made an attempt to outrage her. Thursday evening Ellis was spending the evening at a neighbor's, when fifteen or twenty men called, took him out of the house and applied a coat of tar and feathers. Then, putting a rope around his neck, they proceeded by the use of a rail to convey him to a tree near by. They informed Ellis they were going to hang him. The frightened man prayed and begged for mercy and was finally informed that if he would leave the place he would be liberated. This he promised to do, and on being released immediately left for parts unknown. Ellis is a drunken, dissipated man, about fifty years old. He has been married, but separated from his wife a few years ago and since then has led a vagrant life.
paul-ellis-shrewsbury-1882-07-13.A13: THE SHREWSBURY LYNCHING.—The man Ellis, who came so near being lynched in Shrewsbury, instead of leaving the country went to Rutland, got drunk and was put in jail. Upon examination before the justice on the charge of attempting to commit rape, decision was reserved until Wednesday, when it was rendered that the evidence was not sufficient to warrant his detention. He has been discharged. Henry W. Wilcox, Henry Plumley, John Danvers, Charles Gleason, Patrick Dyer, and Addison Pierce were arrested on charge of having been engaged in the lynching of Ellis. They waived examination and each was put under $250 bonds which was furnished. They seem to be substantial citizens, for each furnished bail for some one of the number.

A Mother Cuts Her Babe's Head Off With a Hatchet—A Kentucky Judge Threatened by a Mob—Some Other Unnatural Exploits.

AN UNNATURAL MOTHER.

VIRGINIA, Nev., Nov. 4.—The wife of Daniel Glassett, a miner, in a fit of insanity, left here night before last, taking with her a babe and two small children. She returned yesterday with the two older children, having been in the mountains all the previous night in a heavy snow storm, explaining that the babe had annoyed her by crying and she had cut its head off with a hatchet. The statement proved true. Officers to-day found the body with the head severed. She has been locked up.

AN IRISH-AFRICAN FEUD.

New York, Nov. 4.—A feud that it is feared will lead to serious results has broken out at Selauket, Long Island, between the colored and Irish people who have recently come into this place in great numbers to work in the rubber factory. A few nights ago a white man was badly beaten by some negroes, and in retaliation the whites beat every colored man they found on the street. Stones and clubs were used, and several persons badly injured. The negro dwellings were attacked and windows and doors broken. The negroes finally appeared armed with shot guns, when their assailants fled, but further trouble is feared.

A JUDGE THREATENED.

A JUDGE THREATENED.

LOUISVILLE, Nov. 4.—Judge Geo. N. Brown, who granted a change of venue in the cases of Neal and Croft at Cattlettsburg, the day before the affair with the mob at Ashland, is at Frankfort, having left his home to avoid the fury of the mob, which friends believed would be directed against him. Citizens of Cattlettsburg offered their services to protect him, but Brown deemed it best to absent himself until the excitement subsided, as he feared that this very offer of protection might lead to a collision between the mob and law-abiding citizens, which he desired to avoid. Prominent citizens of Ashland have telegraphed Brown that the situation has changed and is very quiet. He will return home to-morrow.

FALSE PRETENSES.

DENVER, Nov. 4.—Orrin Skinner, a merchant of Quincy, Ill., was arrested at Idaho Springs to-day for having obtained money under false pretenses. He had a letter of introduction to a mining expert, Frank Asbeston, and on the strength of it secured payment on a draft for $2,500 on a New York bank. He telegraphed immediately and had payment on the draft stopped. He had several thousand dollars on deposit in the Georgetown bank. This fact being evidence of fraudulent intent on his part. On being arrested he restored the $2,500 and paid an additional sum of $500 for expenses.

NEW-YORK CITY.

At one large importing house twenty-four different shapes of ladies' hats are to be found.

Deaths last week 579; births, 536; marriages, 240; arrests, 1,191; excise licenses granted, 83, and fees collected, $4,575.

The amount collected from Croton water rents last week was $31,253.99. There were 1,679 licenses issued and the amount collected was $2,182.

Beginning to-morrow the steamers of the Stonington Line to Boston and of the Providence Line to Providence will leave this city at 4:30 p.m. instead of 5 o'clock.

A BIG FISH ON EXHIBITION.

A large fish, known as the American Angler or Sophius Americanus, caught off Pier No. 19 North River, last week, was on exhibition yesterday in Fulton Market.

FINDING THE PRESIDENT'S SEITER DOG.

A valuable settler dog owned by President Arthur was lost several days ago, and a general alarm, describing it, was sent out to the police. Yesterday a policeman of the Twenty-first Precinct found the animal in First-ave, and returned it to Mr. Arthur's residence.

ASSIGNMENTS MADE YESTERDAY.

The following assignments were filed yesterday in the County Clerk's office: Soiomon Dentz and Simon Sanders to Daviil L. Elsner with preferences to the amount of $2,697; and Edward C. Coggeshall to William R. Spooner with $18,705 preferences.

ARRIVALS OF IMMIGRANTS.

The total number of immigrants landed at Castle Garden during the week ending yesterday was 6,990. Yesterday the steamer Elbe from Bremen brought 1,084 steerage passengers; the Hekla, from Copenhagen, 359; and the Elysia, from the Mediterranean ports, 426.

CUTTING HER THROAT WITH A RAZOR.

Mrs. Eva Schroeder, age sixty, the wife of a poor German tailor at No. 249 West Thirty-fifth-st., committed suicide yesterday by cutting her throat with a razor while her husband was away at work. She had been ill for several years, and vainly had sought relief at Bellevue Hospital.

MADE HOMELESS BY INCENDIARIES.

Flames broke out yesterday in a small goat-house at the foot of West One-hundred-and-twenty-eighth-st., while the occupant was making a tour of the district in search of election posters. Although the Fire Department was summoned promptly, the entire building was destroyed. The youthful owner of the house, "Tommie" McKinney, thought that the fire was of incendiary origin. He estimated his loss at $5, and said there was no insurance.

BROOKLYN.

Mrs. Bridget McGinley, an inmate of the Home for the Aged, died yesterday at the age of 101 years. She came from Ireland thirty-seven years ago.

The Rev. Payson Ingersoll, of the Middle Reformed Church in Harrison-st., has accepted the call to the Puritan Congregational Church at Lafayette and Marcy-aves.

James S. Cole, who died at his home, No. 194 Monroe-st., yesterday, was a nephew of Governor Smallwood, of Marville, and was born in Washington in 1811. For nearly fifty years he has lived in Brooklyn.

A post-mortem examination yesterday showed that the death of Mrs. Rosa Barr, which occurred at No. 16 Garrison-st. recently, after a beating from her husband, resulted from alcoholism. Her husband was discharged from custody.

Joseph Strange, while temporarily deranged, from the loss by fire of his store at No. 470 De Kalb-ave., yesterday fired four shots from a revolver at his head, and one at his body, and he is in a critical state at the Long Island College Hospital.

Health Commissioner Raymond has, after a long hearing, decided that the works of the New-York Cream of Tartar Company, at Kent-ave, and Morton-st., E. D., are not injurious to the public health, by reason of the odors and vapors proceeding from them.

George E. Apsley, a Tarrytown real estate dealer, was arrested yesterday by Detective Zundt on complaint of Franklin M. Tripp, of No. 138 Clermont-ave., charged with stealing a deed of property valued at $4,500. Justice Walsh held him for examination.

Thomas Kelman, sixty-three years of age, living at No. 16 Carlton-ave., was stricken with apoplexy while at work in the pipe-yard of the Board of City Works, in North Portland-ave. yesterday afternoon, and he died within a few minutes, before a physician, who was sent for, could arrive.

Inspector Jewett yesterday detailed a platoon of police, which he promised to command himself if necessary, at the request of Adolph Baker, owner of the Masonic Temple, Grand-st, E. D., to that hall to-night. The Salvation Army have been meeting at the Temple for several Sunday nights past, but the crowd they attracted misused the furniture. Baker sent them notice that they could not meet there anymore. Lieutenant Bain sent back word that if the doors were closed to them to-night, his warriors would batter them down.

JERSEY CITY.

The contest for a seat in the Township Committee of Weehawken between Henry B. Price and John Allen was decided yesterday by Judge Knapp in favor of Mr. Price.

Mrs. Edward G. Bullock, of Erie and Seventh-sts., recovered a diamond earring yesterday which was stolen from her on September 15. The diamond was stolen from Mrs. Bullock's house by Robert Kennedy, a theatre ticket speculator, who called there to collect a bill. Mrs. Bullock put detectives on Kennedy's track, and he was followed so closely that yesterday he sent a friend to see her. His friend took Mrs. Bullock to a pawnbroker's shop in New-York, where the diamond was recovered. Kennedy could not be found by the police.

STATEN ISLAND.

STAPLETON.—The body of an unknown man was fouk yesterday in the bay near the shore in front of the Seamen's Retreat. He was apparently about sixty-five years old, had gray hair and whiskers and a large mole on the left side of his neck. There was a deep wound on the back of his head, from which blood was oozing when the body was taken from the wate. A colored man on one of Parmley's canal boats moored at Stapleton says that he heard cries for help out in the bay on Friday night.

PORT RICHMOND.—Citizens have presented a petition to the trustees of the village, requesting that an ordinance should be passed, prohibiting the blowing of steam whistles within the limits of the village.

NEW-BRIGHTON.—Sneak thieves entered the house of Mr. Stewart, St. Sames's-place, while the family were at dinner, and stole a gold watch, three suits of clothes and $10 in money.

A few nights ago a white man, John Muller, was terribly beaten by several negroes, and his jaw bone was broken. The negro dwellings were attacked and the windows and doors broken. The negroes finally appeared armed with shotguns, when their assailants fled, but further trouble is feared.

ROCKVILLE CENTRE—Henry Beard, age nine, fell into an oyster barrell yesterday while at play. He caught his face on a nail, tearing a gash from eye to eye. It is feared that he will lose his eyesight.

PERSONAL AND GENERAL.
DURING the last trip of the steamer Oceanica from Chicago to Buffalo, N. Y., the boilers broke from their fastenings and the steam and water escaped into the firehold. After an hour's pumping, the body of John Christopher, aged 40, was found lying face downward, where he had probably thrown himself to escape the steam, only to die in the hot water.

JULES ROEDER, a commercial traveler for a St. Louis house, was found dead in bed at the City Hotel, Little Rock, Ark., the other morning. He had been taking morphine for some time, and probably died from an overdose.

LOUISA RAISING, of Fort Dodge, Iowa, a woman with two daughters to care for, hanged herself the other morning rather than pay a heavy fine or undergo imprisonment for selling whisky.

JOHN GLYNN, a negligent flagman, caused a collision of freight trains at Diamond, Pa., Nov. 1, which cost him his life. Several employees were hurt and twenty-five cars were demolished.

A. B. COLE, a lawyer, was killed by a Texas Pacific train near Dallas, Texas, the other morning. As he had been financially embarrassed for some time it is thought he threw himself on the track.

HENRY P. COOPER, a well-known tailor, was sent to a private mad-house in New York the other day at the instance of two brothers, and now a third brother has begun legal proceedings to have him released, claiming him perfectly sane.

The engine-house of Fox & Co.'s woolen factory at Urbana, Ohio, was demolished by a boiler explosion on the 1st, and Robert Outram, the engineer, was badly injured and died in a few hours.

The New York Central freight depot at Rochester, N. Y., and ten cars loaded with merchandise were destroyed by fire the other day. Losses will probably reach $100,000.

ANDREW JACKSON, a negro who had assaulted a little white girl near Vienna, La., was lynched by vigilantes the other day.

The skeleton of a hunter, named Goodenough, who had long been missing from Greenville, Me., was discovered in the woods near Moosehead Lake the other day, fastened in a bear-trap.

A young daughter of J. G. Welsh-
A YOUNG daughter of J. G. Welshaus, of Glen's Falls, W. Va., was fatally burned by the explosion of a lamp the other evening.

PETTY thieves have been annoying farmers near New Richmond, Ohio, for some time. Albert and James Thornton, negroes, were suspected. The other morning they were found lying in a cornfield, riddled with shot and bleeding to death. No one knew anything about the shooting, but the colored people in town became very disorderly in investigating the matter and a number were lodged in jail.

POLICEMAN J. C. PEPPER attempted to arrest Frank Reynolds and Frank Colwell in a saloon at Massillon, Ohio, the other night. Reynolds closed with the officer, and in the tussle that ensued drew a revolver and shot him in the thigh, making a serious wound. With the assistance of bystanders, however, both men were lodged in jail, and the wounded man was attended by a surgeon.

The jury in the case of Dick Liddell, on trial at Huntsville, Ala., for participation in the robbery of Alexander Smith at Mussel Shoals in 1881, returned a verdict of guilty. Liddell proved that he was in Kentucky at the time of the robbery, which, he said, was committed by Frank and Jesse James and Bill Ryan, who were hiding from officers. He admitted that he at other times and places had run and robbed with the bandits. The verdict is a peculiar one. It recites belief in Liddell's statements, but says he is guilty of conspiracy nevertheless. The Court suspended sentence and fixed $1,500 bond for the prisoner's appearance at the next term. The action is said to be taken to avoid fixing on Liddell the imputation of sentence and conviction, as he is a valuable witness in several other cases against the James band, and may also be needed to testify against Frank James, should the latter be put on trial for the Mussel Shoals robbery. It is expected that Liddell will, for this reason, either receive a pardon or that sentence will be indefinitely postponed.

FIRE at Hull, Ontario, the other day, destroyed property valued at $500,000.

A MUTINY occurred on the schooner Dora S. Trimble as she was leaving Boston, Mass., the other day. Hand-spikes and clubs were freely used by the crew, and the captain and mate were seriously injured. The vessel was boarded by harbor police and two of the ring-leaders were arrested.

GREAT forest fires are raging in the Catskills, opposite Germantown, N. Y.

THE Catholic schools at Dubuque, Iowa, have been closed on account of the prevalence of scarlet fever.

The Post-office Department has declared Frank E. Vaif, of Market street, Philadelphia, alias A. S. Arnold, Broadway, New York, with half a dozen aliases in each city, a fraudulent concern. Postmasters are directed not to deliver money-orders or registered letters to him.

J. W. SIMONTON, formerly general agent of the Associated Press in New York, died suddenly from heart disease, near Napa, Cal., on the 2d.

THE Arlington Variety Theater in Baltimore, Md., burned on the 3d. John Pearson, a young man, perished in the flames. Miss Georgie Supple, one of the company, was seriously injured in jumping from the roof. Several others were badly burned or hurt in making their escape.

GEORGE BRIMMER, arrested for setting fire to the Poorhouse barn at Lancaster, Pa., has made a confession implicating eight members of a regularly organized band of incendiaries.

A WHITE MAN was badly beaten by some negroes in Setauket, Long Island, the other night, and in retaliation the whites set upon every black man they found on the streets. The fight became general; stones and clubs were freely used, and several participants were seriously injured. The negro quarters were then attacked, windows and doors broken, and the torch applied; but fire-arms were brought into use and the assailants were driven off.

J. W. WALKER, a ranchman, has been arrested at Denver, Colo., for killing Sam Yaw, a Chinese laundrymen. Walker had been put out of the laundry for attempting to take clothes for which he had no ticket, and he used his pistol on the first heathen at hand, who happened to be an innocent bystander.

MARY MUELLER, aged 70, was run down and killed by a train near San Antonio, Texas, the other night.

SHREVEPORT, La., lost $175,000 by fire on the 5th. A fine block in Red Bank, N. J., including the First National Bank and a Methodist church, went up in smoke on the same day.

A boy named Robinson was decapitated by a cable car in Chicago the other morning.

CHAPMAN's cartridge factory, Suffield, Conn., was destroyed by an explosion of chemicals the other day. James Saunders was fatally injured, Charles Brewster and James Lyons were badly burned, and four others were slightly hurt.

FIVE trainmen were seriously injured in a collision near Pomfret, Conn., caused by violating orders. Two engines and twelve cars were wrecked.

MRS. DANIEL GLASSETT, wife of a miner, wandered off into the mountains near Virginia, Nev., the other day, taking with her an infant and two other children. Having spent the night in a furious snow-storm, she returned without the babe, explaining that it had annoyed her by crying and she had cut its head off with a hatchet. A search for the body verified her story, and she was arrested. Of course she is insane.

JOHN RADFORD, of Belleview, Ohio, has been arrested for the murder of his wife, who had applied for a divorce. She left him because of his intimacy with another woman. He followed her to her father's house, broke down two doors, dragged her into the yard, and shot her twice, in the presence of her children, her mother and sister.

WASHINGTON butchers, dismayed at the success of the competition of Chicago dealers, have instituted legal measures to test the right of the latter to sell meat

Gallathy, of New York; George K. Kelley, Pittsburgh; George K. Hopkins, St. Louis; Samuel J. Hale, Cincinnati, and A. J. Wilkinson, Keokuk, Iowa; Treasurer, S. M.
