Lyons, New Orleans.

Payne, charged with bribery by Juror Brown, was held in the sum of $2,000 for his appearance before the Grand Jury at Washington.

William McLendon, Sam Stafford and William Starr, negroes, were killed by the caving in of a sand bank on the line of the Macon & Brunswick Railroad, near Macon, Georgia, on the 8th.

There were seven new cases of fever and one death at Pensacola on the 7th.

Brevet Major-General Richard Arnold, for a long time on the staff of General Hancock, died at Governor's Island, New
ARNOLD, for a long time on the staff of General Hancock, died at Governor's Island, New York, on the 8th.

A FEMALE inmate of the Erie County, Pa., almshouse was burned to death on the 8th, her clothes catching fire from a pipe she was smoking. She was in a room by herself and, being blind, could not find assistance promptly.

The body of R. T. Simpson, a citizen of Pittsburgh, was found in a pool of blood on Liberty Street, that city, on the morning of the 8th. His face and head were cut and blood had been issuing from his ears and nostrils. It was supposed that he had been murdered in a house near by and the body carried into the street and placed where found. Three women, named Mrs. Wright, Clara Warren and Mrs. Davidson, inmates of a suspected house, were arrested on suspicion of having committed the crime.

A DISPATCH from Albany, N. Y., on the 9th states that the New York and Erie Canal would be closed on December 7.

The Treasury Department on the 9th purchased 418,000 ounces of fine silver for delivery at the United States mints for coinage.

F. N. BASSETT, of Connecticut, has been designated as Acting Chief Clerk of the Post-office Department.

PROFESSOR BAIRD, of Washington, is making arrangements to send to the London Exposition, to be held in May next, an elaborate exhibit of American life-saving apparatus.

FRANK H. SMALL, charged with conspiracy to corrupt the jurymen in the Star route trial, at Washington, was placed under $4,000 bonds on the 9th to await the action of the Grand Jury.

JOHN W. BURNS, proprietor of the Shelbyville, Ind., Volunteer, was shot on the night of the 8th while on his way home from his office by some unknown person. His wound was not serious.

WILLIE EARL, aged twelve years, purchased a revolver, and in company with two other boys of about his own age, attended a variety show at Detroit on the night of the 8th. In the morning he was found dead in a shed with a bullet hole in his forehead. His companions could not be found.

A DISPATCH from New Orleans on the 9th states that Ex-Mayor Nevin, of Adrian, Mich., who absconded some time since with the proceeds of the sale of bonds of that city which he had unlawfully sold in New York had been captured at El Paso, Texas, and would be taken back to Michigan for trial. The $3,000 reward offered for his capture expired by limitation on the 5th.

THERE were nine new cases of fever and two deaths at Pensacola on the 9th. The total number of cases to date were 2,319 and 190 deaths.

TEN of the principal business houses in Neola, Iowa, were destroyed by fire on the night of the 8th. Loss $40,000; partly insured.

THE General Assembly of Georgia, on the 9th, elected Samuel Hall Judge of the Supreme Court of that State, vice A. M. Spencer, whose term had expired.

LEE, BLOOM & Co., wholesale liquor dealers of Louisville, Ky., made an assignment on the 9th. Liabilities $70,000; assets $50,000.

A DELEGATION of members of the Pennsylvania Historical Society went from Philadelphia to Chester, Pa., on the 9th, and erected with appropriate ceremonies a monumental stone on the spot where William Penn landed when he first came to this country.

A FIGHT occurred between the colored and Irish portion of the population of Setauket, Long Island, on the night of the 9th, during which two men and a woman were badly cut with a razor in the hands of Stephen Johnson. A white man named Muller had his jaw broken and Samuel Smith, colored, was terribly clubbed. The combatants were rival operators in a rubber factory at that place, and a fancied injury was the cause of the trouble.

THE Catholic clergy of the Archdiocese of New York met in St. Patrick's Cathedral, that city, on the 9th, for the purpose of holding a diocesan synod. The session was formally opened with mass, the celebrant being Archbishop Coningan, assisted by Fathers Lavelle and Kelley. Cardinal McCloskey presided over the meeting, which was held with closed doors.

CHARLES H. GARBER, a member of the family poisoned at Norristown, Pa., recently, by eating pie containing arsenic, died on the 9th. Some of the flour from which the pie was made has been found to contain arsenic-in crystals of purer quality than usually sold by druggists. Foul play is suspected.

THE public schools of Birdsboro, Pa., closed on the 9th, owing to the prevalence of scarlet fever and diphtheria. In one family five children had died, and the disease was on the increase.

THE Globe Rubber Company, of Trenton, N. J., failed on the 9th. Liabilities $175,000; assets $120,000.

THE Methodist Episcopal Mission, in session at New York on the 9th, appropriated the following sums for missions in the United States not in the conference: Arizona, $8,000; Black Hills, $3,600; Dakota, $5,500; Indian Territory, $2,000; Montana, $11,000; New Mexico $12,500; Utah, $12,500; Norwegian and Swedish missions, California, $2,200.

The Census Bureau has given a bulletin on statistics of the manufacture of petroleum during the census year ending May 31, 1880, which shows that there were eighty-six corporations engaged in this industry, $27,395,746 in capital invested; 9,809 hands employed, to whom $4,381,572 in wages were paid. The total value of raw material used was $34,996,101; the value of the manufactured products being $43,705,218.

THE sawmill of E. John, with a large quantity of lumber, a warehouse and dwelling, were burned at Point Pleasant, W. Va., on the 9th. Loss $15,000; no insurance except on the dwelling.

THE production of ale and beer in Cincinnati, Covington and Newport, according to the report of Superintendent Maxwell, of the Chamber of Commerce, during the year ending September 1, amounted to 827,281 barrels, which is 90,000 barrels more than in the previous year. The production in Cincinnati was 769,621, which is an increase of sixty-four per cent. in seven years.

ACTING SECRETARY JOSLYN decided a case on the 10th that when a husband and wife were voluntarily divorced, in order that the wife might make the entry of the land under the homestead laws, and the woman subsequently lived with the divorced husband, the decision holds that in consequence thereof the woman cannot be considered the head of the family within the meaning of the law, and the land entry is fraudulent.

THE Supreme Court of Rhode Islan

saloon-murderer-logan.A1: A World correspondent visiting the Mormons has found a great deal to admire in their social life, and writes a flattering account of one of their settlements, called Logan, a place of four thousand inhabitants, where every man owns his farm, and where there are only two policemen, who have so little to do that they engage in other business. It is not because of their business. It is not because of their polygamous practices, however, that these Mormon settlers maintain good order without the intervention of the people. In fact the proportion of polygamists is very small. The population is select; in the first place, as to the sobriety, industry and thrifty habits of its members. Then, too, they have banished liquor from the settlement. When liquor was sold there a murder was committed in a drinking saloon, and these now orderly townfolks lynched the murderer and abolished the liquor traffic. After a time licenses were again issued, and there were soon ten times as many prisoners in tail as before the opening of saloons. The latter were then definitely closed, with the result that Logan cannot find full employment for its police force of two men. Polygamy, or the absence of it, has nothing whatever to do with this—in fact, there are other settlements, such as Vineland, where similarly good results were obtained; first, by the thrifty habits of the people, and next, by forbidding the sale of liquor.

St. Louis Wheat Market.

St. Louis, Mo., August 10—The directors of the Merchants Exchange fixed $1.18½ as the selling price for June wheat, and adding five per cent. damages for not using proper diligence in filling contracts. This makes the price nearly $1.24½.

From the Seat of War.

Constantinople, August 10—The sultan has issued a proclamation declaring Arabi Pasha a rebel. He condemns the conduct of the military leaders as rebellious and criminal and mentions the friendly relations of the porte with England.

DOMESTIC.
A lad named James Henry was drowned in the Ohio River, opposite Cincinnati. Patrick McCarthy volunteered to dive for the lad, and in so doing, was also drowned.

Five persons were drowned by the capsize of a boat at Nantucket, Mass.

Drouth is complained of in Massachusetts and other portions of the East.

Rufus Hatch and a party of English and New York capitalists have purchased 750,000 acres of grazing lands, lying between the Little Missouri and Powder rivers, in Montana, from the Northern Pacific Road, at $1 per acre, on seven years' time. As the grant to the road only takes alternate sections, the syndicate will have a practical pasturage of 1,500,000 acres, as it will have the use of the intervening sections of government land. It is proposed to stock it with 50,000 head of cattle. The party, in company with Herman Trott, Land Commissioner of the Northern Pacific, are now en route to inspect this purchase.

A Mount Airy, N. C., dispatch of August 8, relates the following concerning the proposed tramp of six frolicsome young ladies: "Six gay and frolicsome young ladies arrived in this place to-day, all rigged out and equipped for a journey on foot through the mountains of this State. The girls wear dresses even shorter than the regulation walking suit, have knapsacks strapped over their shoulders, wear broad-bottomed easy shoes, dark hose, and are fixed up for comfort. They propose to take a trip on foot through all of the mountain counties of North Carolina. In their baggage they have hammocks, which will be used in case they will have to camp out at night. The trip will consume about two months, and cover a district of six or eight hundred miles. The girls are all young, the oldest probably not over 22, and the youngest 16."

HUNDREDS of letters received by business houses at St. Louis from correspondents throughout the South, Southwest and West say that there never have been such crops of corn and oats raised in Texas, Arkansas, Mississippi, Alabama, Tennessee, the Indian Territory, Missouri and Kansas as those of the present season.

A severe storm prevailed along the eastern part of Massachusetts, August 8, extending into Maine. A number of dwellings and many barns were struck by lightning and destroyed, involving considerable loss.

JAMES ROBERT ADAMS, cashier of the West End Hotel, Long Branch, killed himself. Domestic trouble is the cause assigned.

FIVE persons were killed in a railroad accident near Pittsburg Station, Texas.

BROWNSVILLE, Texas, reported fifty cases of yellow fever on the 9th.

PAUL TOLLNER, at Chicago, murdered his young wife and then killed himself.

SAM MILLER, a negro, was taken from the Newnan jail, Georgia, by seventy masked men, and hanged. His crime was that of attempting to outrage a white woman, in Campbell County.

GEORGE B. HAMILTON, aged nineteen years, who is bookkeeper of the Farmers' Bank, Wyoming, Illinois, has absconded with $3,000 of the bank's funds.

SUITS for damages amounting to $70,000 have already been begun by administrators of persons killed in the Scioto disaster against the Wheeling and Parkersburg Transportation Company.

A PREMATURE blast at Cornwall, New York, on the West Shore Road, killed four negroes and wounded several others.

tle of Wilson's Creek (Mo.), where General Lyon was killed, was celebrated on the 10th. General Pope and others made speeches. PERSONAL AND POLITICAL.

NASHVILLE, Tenn., Nov. 6 — A riot occurred here to-night in Cherry-st. While the Republican Legislative nominees were speaking, a street-car passed though the crowd knocking down an old colord man, Alfred King by name, and inflicting injuries which caused his death an hour later. Nearly 1,000 negroes seized Benjamin Woodward, the street-car driver, and hundreds of knives and pistols were out. Constable Dowdey (colored) held the crowd at bay until the arrival of police although seriously cut and knocked down several times.

The riot signal was rung, and a large number of citizens protected the retreat of the police and their prisoner, although shouts of "hang him," "shoot him" "throw him off the bridge" were heard.

The prisoner was taken to jail, having a finger broken and being cut in several places with knives. Police were also knocked down and otherwise maltreated. w-h-yeats-chatham-1882-07-29.A6:
CHATHAM.
HOW YEATT'S RESPIE WAS RECEIVED—A
PLAIN STATEMENT OF FACTS—THE PRISONER'S CONFESSIONS, &C.
To-day was the day fixed upon for the execution of Yeatts for the murder of young Adkerson, but on yesterday Special Messenger T. E. Drinkard arrived from Richmond and delivered to Sheriff Overby a respite of the sentence until Friday, August 4th. In anticipation, however, that the execution would take place to-day, a number of persons from various sections of the county came to town with the hope of seeing the prisoner on his way to the gallows; but though disappointed in this, they were not entirely unrewarded, as occasionally they got a glimpse of the doomed man as he looked out on the street through the iron bars of his cell.

Surprise was expressed by some at the action of the Governor, as they appeared to think it indicative of still further leniency towards the prisoner, but the general opinion was that upon an investigation of the matter the Governor would not interfere with the verdict of the jury, which, upon an appeal, has been approved by the highest court of the State. It was stated in the Dispatch several days ago that among the grounds urged to the Governor for clemency by Major Yeatts, the father of the condemned man, and Mr. D. H. Pannili, who accompanied him, were that at the time of the trial the father was confined to his bed from sickness; that the prisoner made a poor defence and had no one to assist him until his father recovered, which was only a week or so ago; and, furthermore, that a great change in the public sentiment of the county had set in in favor of the prisoner under the light of recent events.

The facts are that Major Yeatts, at the time the murder was committed, was confined to his bed from sickness, but was present during the whole time of his son's trial, and was up and going about for more than a month prior thereto. He employed as able counsel to defend his son as he could have gotten in this section—to wit, Mr. Robert H. Tredway, of this place, and Messrs. Peatross and Harriss, of Danville, and it is said by those able to judge that considering the one-sidedness of the case they made a very able and ingenious defence. There were twenty-three witnesses summoned for the defence, and out of this number but barely one was examined.

In regard to a change having taken place in the sentiment of the people, this is so; but that change is decidedly against the prisoner. Among a few there has been, and perhaps is now, some small sympathy for him, but this last attempt of his to leave a stain on the character of his wife is regarded by the great majority of right-thinking people of the county as the crowning act of infamy to a life already black with crime.

For weeks before his trial he was besought by his counsel if he had any reason to suspect any undue intimacy between young Adkerson and his wife either before or after his marriage to speak out; in fact, they told him that the only way to save his neck from the gallows was to use some such argument, but he declared to the last that he had no ground for such a suspicion, and that young Adkerson was one of the best friends he ever had.

Within the last few weeks, however, he has made a confession—in fact, a half a dozen or more—two written ones and the others to various persons who have conversed with him, every one of which is different. In the first one made to his counsel, Mr. Tredway, written and signed by himself, he declares substantially as follows:

That Adkerson came to him a week before his marriage and asked him if he considered him his friend; that he told him yes; that Adkerson said then, "As a friend, I advise you not to marry Miss Rorer; if you do you will a —" ; that he said to Adkerson, "Do you know that to be a fact"; that he replied, "No, but I have heard it"; that he then said to Adkerson, "You are a liar," and that Adkerson said. "You must retract that or one of us must die," and that he replied, "Let slip, I'm ready"; that at this point they were interrupted by some one coming up, and ceased their conversation; that the next day after his marriage he went to Sycamore, and said to Adkerson, "I want you to repeat what you said the other day"; that Adkerson declined, and requested him to walk down the railroad track, and they would settle it; that they walked down the track a piece, and he requested Adkerson to retract what he had said, and he refused, and said he would die before he would do so; that he (Yeatts) pulled out his pistol, and that Adkerson said to him, "You are not going to shoot me with that pistol"; that he thereupon placed it to his head and fired, and that Adkerson's lifeless body rolled down the bank; that the articles belonging to Adkerson found upon his (Yeatts)'s person when captured were given to him by Adkerson to keep for him before he killed him; that after killing him he took the train for Tennessee.

In his other written confession, which he has requested should not be published until he has "shuffled off this mortal coil," I am told that he declares that he killed Adkerson in order to get from him the forged due bill, which he (Yeatts) had sold him some time before, on T. L. Poindexter & Son, of Danville; that after killing him he took from him his safe-key and various other articles and started towards Adkerson's store to get from the safe the due bill, but expecting that he would meet with resistance, and having only three bullets left in his pistol, he decided to walk to the next station and there take the train, which he did. His other statements, it is said, differ as widely as these two. Taking the best view of the case, he is guilty of a wilful and most atrocious murder.

In regard to the affidavits which have been laid before the Governor tending to show that there was an improper intimacy existing between Adkerson and Yeatts's wife, it is thought here that there has been some crookedness in their procurement, though they may be bona-fide documents. It was proved, however, upon the trial that young Adkerson had not been to Mr. Rorer's house but twice during the past year, and that these visits were eight or nine months apart, and that he only had a friendly neighborhood acquaintance with Miss Rorer. A petition has been circulated by Major Yeatts remote from where the crime was committed, and a good many persons have signed it through sympathy for him, who is now an old man, bowed down by grief; but even many of these declare that Yeatts deserves to be hung.

The father has the most profound respect and sympathy, and though his son has committed a great crime, and will no doubt pay the forfeit upon the gallows, the father will still be respected among all

CHATHAM, VA., August 4.—Walter Hamilton Yeatts was hanged here to-day for the murder of Presley E. Adkerson in February last. The execution was private, being witnessed only by the officers of the court, special guards, physicians, and the press representatives. Everything was quiet and orderly, notwithstanding the fact that a large concourse of people from the surrounding country was in town.

THE CRIME
for which Yeatts was executed was the murder of Presley E. Adkerson, a young merchant and depôt-master at Sycamore station, whose body was found near that place last February with a bullet-hole through the head. Since the conviction of Yeatts he has made two written statements confessing the murder. Before his trial and conviction, and most of the time since, Yeatts was engaged in writing a book, which he gave to his father for publication. It embraces sketches of his career, and is to be entitled “Life and History of W. H. Yeatts; or, A Step to Ruin.” In it he attributes his fall to liquor and women, and asserts that three young ladies in the county, whose names he gives, have fallen victims to his deceptive arts. This morning he retracted that assertion about two of the young ladies, but as to the third he would say nothing.

He left full instructions with Mr. Pigg, editor of the Chatham Tribune, in relation to the

PUBLICATION OF HIS BOOK.

He requested that he be executed in a blue flannel suit, and that his body be encased in a metallic coffin with a glass face and be placed in an upright position in a cemented grave with steps leading down into it so that those who wished to see him "lying in state" could do so.

He desired also that a handkerchief be tied around his neck to hide the traces of the rope, and that a cross of flowers be placed on his breast. He requested, further, that his funeral sermon be preached from the 21st and 22d verses of the xxiii. chapter of Luke.

During his entire confinement his demeanor was calm and composed. He never displayed emotion of any sort. When informed yesterday that the Governor had decided to let the law take its course he received the announcement with unconcern, and said he would prefer death to confinement in the penitentiary. Yesterday evening he made quite

AN ELABORATE TOILET.

He took a bath, and had a barber shave him. He then donned his burial suit, with clean white shirt, standing collar, and black silk scarf.

His father, brother, and brother-in-law visited him last night, and after spending about an hour in his cell took final leave of him. He assured them that he was prepared to die. This morning when visited the condemned man was found seated at a small table reading a Bible as he had been in the habit of doing daily for a month past. He said that he had rested well during the night, having slept five and a half hours. During the morning hours he was visited by a number of people, to all of whom he had something to say. About 10 o'clock Rev. W. A. Alrich, of the Episcopal Church, went into his cell and spent some time with Yeatts, praying and administering

RELIGIOUS CONSOLATION.

At a few minutes after 11 o'clock he was taken from the jail to the scaffold, which was in an enclosure about one hundred yards in rear of the court-house. The march to the scaffold was somewhat impeded by the crowd which blocked the way—all eager to get a sight of the prisoner.

Yeatts was escorted by Sheriff Overby and his assistants. He ascended the platform, and in a few minutes everything was in readiness for the final act of the tragedy.

In reply to a question if he had anything to say he answered distinctly, "No, sir; nothing at all." A WHITE CLOTH WAS THEN TIED OVER HIS FACE and the rope adjusted, after which Sheriff Overby asked if he was ready, and prisoner said, "Give me a minute to think." This was done, Yeatts meanwhile standing erect, with his head slightly bowed, seemingly engaged in prayer.

At 11:21 o'clock the sheriff pulled a lever attached to the bolts of the trap, and in an instant Yeatts was swinging five and a half feet below where he had previously stood. His struggles were not violent but spasmodic; contractions were visible for several minutes; pulsations ceased in ten minutes,
die; contractions were visible for several minutes; pulsations ceased in ten minutes, and at the end of sixteen minutes Dr. Martin pronounced life extinct. At 11:40 the body was taken down and placed in a neat IMITATION ROSEWOOD COFFIN, with white metal handles and neat interior trimmings.

An examination showed that he had died from strangulation. About an hour afterwards the remains were turned over to his brother-in-law, who took them to the family burial-place, some miles distant.

After the execution the crowd turned their attention to the circus, which had just entered the town, and Yeatts and his crime were for the time forgotten.

Some time since Yeatts wrote quite a long poetic effusion of a blasphemous and sacrilligious character, and on the day after he was respited by the Governor, on being informed that a party of men had come to the jail to lynch him but had abandoned the idea, he wrote the following:

Aroused from slumber by the tread of horses
Which came thundering round my cell,
I listened to learn their riders' voices,
Which said they would land me into h-1.
w-h-yeats-chatham-1882-07-29.A12:
not aware that he had an enemy, were at a loss to conjecture the identity of the murderer, but circumstances gradually developed soon after the killing became known which pointed unmistakably to Walter H. Yeatts, a twenty-six-year-old son of Major Charles W. Yeatts, who was formerly a district internal-revenue collector, and also a commission merchant in Lynchburg, Va. Young Yeatts was thought to have been on terms of friendly and familiar intercourse with Adkerson, for it was known that the latter had often befriended him pecuniarily and in other ways. What pointed suspicion at Yeatts was the fact that he was married on February 1st (the day before the murder) to a Miss Fannie Rorer, who lived near Sycamore, and that on the next day he told his wife that he was going away for three weeks to work on the New-River railroad. He then left, and it appeared from after developments that he repaired to Sycamore, and by some representations induced Adkerson to take a walk with him up the railroad track towards Lynchburg. Shortly thereafter a pistol-shot was heard, but no attention was paid to the circumstance, as pistol-shooting thereabouts was no uncommon thing. The next morning, however,

ADKERSON'S BODY WAS FOUND
as described, with a hole through the head made by a bullet, which entered behind one ear and passed out near the other. The tracks about the murdered man, which plainly showed in the snow, were identified as those of Yeatts, and his sudden disappearance led to his being pursued. On the 5th of February he was arrested at Goodson-Bristol, on the Virginia and Tennessee border, and, though giving another name, was soon after identified by Pittsylvania county officers and brought back to the jail at Chatham; not, however, before the excited citizens of the neighborhood had made threats and some preparations to lynch the murderer. When arrested Yeatts was found in possession of Adkerson's pistol, safe-key, and two rings which he had taken from him after killing him. He also had some money which was believed to belong to his victim. His trial occurred at the May term of the County Court, and resulted in his conviction and sentence to be hanged on the 28th of July.

Among the representations which have been made in connection with the affair as showing the cause or

PROVOCATION FOR THE MURDER

is one that when Yeatts was engaged to Miss Rorer, Adkerson expressed regrets to her that she was going to marry a man who was dishonest, and who would after their marriage go to the penitentiary. The cause of this statement was due to the fact that Yeatts had passed on Adkerson for goods and money a bogus check for $75, to which the name of Thomas L. Poindexter & Co., of Danville, was forged, and that he had also tried to impose similar bogus paper on other business-men. It is also stated that Miss Rorer has sustained unlawful relations with Adkerson; that Yeatts knew it, and had been paid by Adkerson to marry the girl; and again, that he discovered her unchasteness only on marriage, and was led to suspect by remarks of Adkerson, who obtruded himself in the company of Yeatts and wife, that they had had guilty relations.

Whether Yeatts was moved to kill Adkerson by innate wickedness or from dread of punishment for committing the alleged forgeries, or from sudden fury at reflecting that Adkerson had been unduly intimate with his wife, must be left to conjecture.

A WEEK'S RESPIE.

A few days before, the day fixed by the Court for the execution of Yeatts his father submitted various papers to Governor Cameron, embracing evidence claimed to be of an extinguating character, accompanied by affidavits, which had not been introduced at the trial. The Governor therefore respited Yeatts for one week (until today), so that he could have time to look into the matter. After a careful investigation he decided not to interfere, but to let the law take its course.

For weeks before his trial he was besought by his counsel if he had any reason to suspect any undue intimacy between young Adkerson and his wife either before or after his marriage to speak out: in fact, they told him that the only way to save his neck from the gallows was to use some such argument, but he declared to the last that he had no ground for such a suspicion, and that young Adkerson was one of the best friends he ever had.

Yeatts's Last Confession.

Since his conviction, however, Yeatts has made two written confessions which conflict materially, as all his statements in connection with the murder have done. The last one he gave to Mr. L. H. Pigg, editor of the Chatham Tribune, with the request that it should not be made public until the day of his execution. In this he speaks of his intimate and friendly relations with Adkerson, the two having "lived together as brothers" for some time previous to his marriage.

On the Sunday before he was married he says: I went to Mr. Rorer's to see my intended wife, and while there she told me Mr. Adkerson had written a letter to her, in which he stated that I was living at Sycamore in danger, and that he was very sorry that she was going to marry me; that after marrying me I would have to leave her and go to the penitentiary for a forgery I had committed in signing Silverthorn's name to a paper which purported to pay me a large sum for a stone I had in my possession.

I remarked to her

I WOULD KILL HIM

unless he retracted for slandering me. I afterwards quieted down, and think I promised her not to say anything more about it. I went back to Sycamore that Sunday night, and as I had been given the privilege of going anywhere in the store as though it belonged to me, I went and armed myself with a large pistol which he left in the store.

On Monday morning we started together for Lynchburg, and directly after we boarded the train I went to him and demanded an explanation. Before I gave him a chance to reply I called him a damned scoundrel and told him he had been to Mr. Rorer's and taken advantage of me, and if he made the same statement to me that he did to them one or the other of us would have to die. He seemed to be very much surprised, and denied having said anything at all. I told him if that be so I retracted what I said about him. He insisted that he had said nothing against me, but that he was as good a friend as I had on earth. Upon this we settled the matter and went on as friends.
w-h-yeats-chatham-1882-07-29.A13: Walter Hamilton Yeatts, a white murderer who was hung last Friday at Chatham, Virginia, was a high toned criminal. He made a special request that his body be laid in a metallic coffin, with a glass face, and be placed in an upright position in a cemented grave, with steps leading down to it, so that those who wished to might see him "lying in state." He also desired that a handkerchief be tied around his neck to hide all traces of the rope, and that a cross of flowers be placed on his breast. His requests about the flowers were observed, but his remains are not as yet lying in state in a cemented grave. His father was formerly Internal Revenue Collector in Lynchburg.

The Alhambra Theater in London was destroyed by fire last night shortly after the close of the performance. Three hundred persons are thrown out of employment.

Deputy Marshals Davis and Farmer, who went to the mountains in Kentucky to seize an illicit distillery, were attacked by a party of thirty moonshiners, and driven twenty-five miles to Frenchburg, but escaped unhurt.

An attempt was made Tuesday night to lynch a white man named W. S. Sims, who is confined in the Alken county, S. C., jail upon a charge of committing a shameful crime upon his own wife. The jail is closely guarded by the state troops under orders from Gov. Thompson. The prisoner is a practising physician.

A young lady lately banished to Siberia for complicity in the nihilist conspiracy has killed the governor of the Transbaikal territory.

In the case of John Devoy, on trial in New York charged with libelling August Belmont, the jury were unable to agree and were locked up last night.

The third game of chess of the new series between Steinitz and Martinez, in Philadelphia, was played last evening and resulted in a draw.

The attorneys for Mrs. Slayback have filed notice of a civil suit for $5,000 damages against Col. Cockerill for killing Col. Slayback in St. Louis.

The body of Capt. Fritz, of the lost steamer Cedar Grove, was found by divers yesterday at the wreck.

A snow storm of especial severity is prevailing in Scotland. Railroad communication is interrupted.

Edward Jacques, the Philadelphia robber, was convicted yesterday morning, and Charles Jacques was convicted as receiver. Thomas Gardiner was also convicted as receiver. Edward Jacques and Gardiner got five years and ten months each. Charles Jacques was held for sentence, and the woman who claims to be Jacques' wife was discharged.

D. M. Bennett, editor of the New York Truth-Seeker, died yesterday.

McCreery & Bender, of Chicago, a stock-yard firm, have failed for $20,000.

Allendale, S. C., by a vote of five to one has declared against license to sell liquor.

The St. Nicholas Bank of New York and the National Bank of New York have determined to become state banks.

Counterfeit five-dollar notes of the Bank of Nova Scotia and the National Bank of Troy, N. Y., are in circulation in Montreal and in other parts of Canada.

Mr. Albert O. Newton, a well-known citizen of New Castle county, Del., died yesterday, aged 85 years. He was related to Gen. Newton, and his eldest brother was a commodore in the U. S. navy.

In the case of C. M. Terrel, chief clerk in the pension agency at Indianapolis, charged with forgeries and conspiracy to defraud the government, the jury returned a verdict of guilty on the fifth and sixth counts.

Maine, which does not punish murder by hanging, has had 11 homicides within the past two years.

A boy under arrest in Wheeling, W. Va., on the charge of incendiarism, curiously enough bears the name of Hotfire.
w-s-sims-aiken-1882-12-06.A4:
A DOCTOR'S DISGRACE.
He is Threatened With Lynching.
From the New York Herald, Dec. 1. A prominent physician of Akron county.
A prominent physician of Alken county, S. C., W. S. Sims, was arrested at Langley last Tuesday on a charge of having committed a diabolical crime against his own wife. The trial justice found some difficulty in specifying it in the warrant of arrest, but the doctor was brought to Alken on complaint of his wife and committed to jail. As soon as the crime became generally known the question was freely discussed in the streets whether it would not be the proper thing to take Sims from the jail and lynch him. The advocates of this method of punishing the prisoner were largely in the majority, and the sheriff, fearing their threats would be executed, telegraphed to the governor for military assistance to protect the accused. Governor Thompson promptly telegraphed Capt. Williams, of the Palmetto Guards, to render the sheriff aid in case it should be needed. Last night about an hour past midnight a band of men, armed and mounted, marched toward Alken for the avowed purpose of lynching Sims. The military company was placed on duty near the jail, and the lynchers were warned not to attempt to capture the prisoner. Some old citizens met the lynchers and demonstrated with them, urging them not to attack the jail, as bloodshed would result. This argument quieted the mob, and they reluctantly returned to their homes. Tonight another party of men will repeat the attempt to lynch Sims, but the military will remain on duty all night to frustrate their designs. There is much excitement in frustrate the Alken over the affair, and the feeling in against Sims is very bitter.

w-s-sims-aiken-1882-12-06.A8:
A NAMELESS CRIME. —Aiken, Dec. 6
—Our jail was guarded last night by the Palmetto Riflemen in consequence of a dispatch from Gov. Thompson to Capt. W. W. Williams, ordering him to report to Sheriff M. T. Holly. It is again guarded to right.

The prisoner whose life is in jeopardy is Dr. W. S. Sims, formerly of Union county, but for many years a practicing physician at Vanieluse, and more recently at Langley, in this county. This man married a young lady of Elgefield county, a Miss Dorn, the daughter of the late proprietor of Dorn's Gold Mine. His offense is against her, and the affidavit upon which the warrant was issued and sworn to by her before Trial Justice Southall, of Langley.

The crime with which he is charged finds no precedent in the books and is unprovided for by the law.

A simple publication of the words of the affidavits would so defile the pages of the News and Courier that the stain could never be exhunged.

The pulse of the community is at fever heat with indignation. —Last night a body of lynchers to the number of over one hundred, said to have come from Graniteville and Langley, made their appearance on the suburbs, buts when informed of the preparation of the prisoner and jail by the Sheriff, they gave up the expedition and returned to their homes. Sheriff Holly is determined to discharge his duty to the last extremity.

The prisoner is to have a preliminary examination on Tuesday next at Langley. The members of the Aiken bar have refused to represent him. Sims is an intelligent man and respectably connected.
w-s-sims-aiken-1882-12-06.A11:
An Unmentionable Crime.
Dr. S. W. Sims, of Aiken County, committed an offense against his wife, for the punishment of which there is no law laid down. The incensed people of Aiken attempted to lynch the brute, but the Governor ordered a militia company to guard the jail, and the lynchers were foiled in their purpose. Sims has been removed to Columbia for safe keeping. The Columbia correspondent of the News and Courier under date of the 12 inst., says:

Dr Sims, the story of whose horrible crime has spread throughout the country, was brought to Columbia to-day from Aiken by Sheriff Holly and his deputy and lodged in jail for safekeeping. His removal from Aiken was made by order of Judge Aldrich as a precautionary measure. The report is that a posse have been organized in Edge field and Augusta for his seizure from the authorities in Aiken and execution by a mob.

Sheriff Holley had no difficulty in transferring his prisoner to Columbia, where he is now safely incarcerated. Sheriff Rowan will take all necessary steps to secure the safety of his prisoner, and there is little danger now that any rescue will be atten- pted.

Sims told the Sheriff to night that his treatment was only the result of political persecution, although so far as known he has not denied to anyone the charges against him. Mr David Johnson, who has been retained for Sims' defense by his friends and connections in Union, arrived in Columbia this evening and will have a conference with the prisoner tomorrow.

Sims told the sheriff to night that he wanted also to secure the services of Col. Abrey for his defence. No one has been allowed to see the prisoner yet, but he is reported to be very uncommunicative and badly frightened.
